domain: Section 3: Ensuring the successful operation of a cloud solution

questions.title: Who deleted the VM yesterday
questions.summary: Who did what and when is an admin activity audit log question.
questions.question: You must determine which user deleted a specific VM instance yesterday afternoon. Where should you look?

options.A: Create a Cloud Asset Inventory feed that publishes asset changes to Pub/Sub.
options.B: Query the BigQuery billing export.
options.C: Query Cloud Logging for the relevant audit log entries.
options.D: Use Cloud Asset Inventory to search all resources across the organisation.

explanation.summary: Who did what and when is an audit-log question: Admin Activity logs record the principal and the API call, which asset inventory does not.

option_breakdown.A: An asset feed reacts to changes as they happen; it does not answer a question about current state.
option_breakdown.B: Billing data describes spend, not configuration, so it cannot say how a resource is configured.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Who did what and when is an audit-log question: Admin Activity logs record the principal and the API call, which asset inventory does not.
option_breakdown.D: Asset search answers 'what exists and how is it configured' right now; it is not a cost tool, a log store, or a change-notification mechanism.

questions.title: Smoke-test a revision before any traffic
questions.summary: Deploying with --tag and --no-traffic publishes a revision at a dedicated URL.
questions.question: A new Cloud Run revision must be smoke-tested by QA on its own URL before any production traffic reaches it. What should you do?

options.A: Update the service's traffic split across revisions by percentage.
options.B: Deploy the new revision with a tag and no traffic, then shift traffic explicitly.
options.C: Route 100% of traffic back to the previously known-good revision.
options.D: Set the container concurrency on the service.

explanation.summary: Deploying with --tag and --no-traffic publishes the revision at a dedicated tagged URL while production continues on the current revision.

option_breakdown.A: Traffic splitting distributes requests across existing revisions; it does not deploy new code or change concurrency.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Deploying with --tag and --no-traffic publishes the revision at a dedicated tagged URL while production continues on the current revision.
option_breakdown.C: Rolling back re-points traffic at an older revision; it does not create a canary or change resource settings.
option_breakdown.D: Concurrency shapes how many requests each instance handles at once; it does not control which revision serves traffic.

questions.title: Send 10 percent to the new revision
questions.summary: Cloud Run splits traffic across revisions by percentage.
questions.question: After validation, 10% of live traffic should go to the new Cloud Run revision while the remainder stays on the old one. What should you do?

options.A: Set the container concurrency on the service.
options.B: Set minimum and maximum instance counts on the service.
options.C: Update the service's traffic split across revisions by percentage.
options.D: Deploy the new revision with a tag and no traffic, then shift traffic explicitly.

explanation.summary: Cloud Run splits traffic across revisions by percentage, which is how a gradual rollout is expressed.

option_breakdown.A: Concurrency shapes how many requests each instance handles at once; it does not control which revision serves traffic.
option_breakdown.B: Instance bounds control cold starts and the scaling ceiling; they say nothing about revisions or traffic.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Cloud Run splits traffic across revisions by percentage, which is how a gradual rollout is expressed.
option_breakdown.D: Tagging a revision without traffic validates a release before exposing it; it is not how you roll back or change scaling.

questions.title: Error rates spike after a release
questions.summary: Previous revisions are retained, so shifting traffic back restores service in seconds.
questions.question: Error rates spike immediately after a Cloud Run release. You need the fastest safe action to restore service. What should you do?

options.A: Deploy the new revision with a tag and no traffic, then shift traffic explicitly.
options.B: Update the service's traffic split across revisions by percentage.
options.C: Set the container concurrency on the service.
options.D: Route 100% of traffic back to the previously known-good revision.

explanation.summary: Because previous revisions are retained, sending 100% of traffic back to the last good revision restores service in seconds without a rebuild.

option_breakdown.A: Tagging a revision without traffic validates a release before exposing it; it is not how you roll back or change scaling.
option_breakdown.B: Traffic splitting distributes requests across existing revisions; it does not deploy new code or change concurrency.
option_breakdown.C: Concurrency shapes how many requests each instance handles at once; it does not control which revision serves traffic.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Because previous revisions are retained, sending 100% of traffic back to the last good revision restores service in seconds without a rebuild.

questions.title: Connection pool exhausted under load
questions.summary: Lowering container concurrency bounds simultaneous requests, and so connections, per instance.
questions.question: A Cloud Run service opens one database connection per request and begins failing under load with connection-pool exhaustion, although CPU is fine. What should you change?

options.A: Set the container concurrency on the service.
options.B: Route 100% of traffic back to the previously known-good revision.
options.C: Set minimum and maximum instance counts on the service.
options.D: Deploy the new revision with a tag and no traffic, then shift traffic explicitly.

explanation.summary: Lowering container concurrency reduces the number of simultaneous requests per instance, which directly bounds the connections each instance opens.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Lowering container concurrency reduces the number of simultaneous requests per instance, which directly bounds the connections each instance opens.
option_breakdown.B: Rolling back re-points traffic at an older revision; it does not create a canary or change resource settings.
option_breakdown.C: Instance bounds control cold starts and the scaling ceiling; they say nothing about revisions or traffic.
option_breakdown.D: Tagging a revision without traffic validates a release before exposing it; it is not how you roll back or change scaling.

questions.title: Cold starts after idle periods
questions.summary: A minimum instance count keeps containers warm so post-idle requests avoid a cold start.
questions.question: Users complain about latency on the first request after a quiet period. The team accepts paying to keep some capacity warm. What should you change?

options.A: Deploy the new revision with a tag and no traffic, then shift traffic explicitly.
options.B: Set minimum and maximum instance counts on the service.
options.C: Update the service's traffic split across revisions by percentage.
options.D: Route 100% of traffic back to the previously known-good revision.

explanation.summary: Setting a minimum number of instances keeps containers warm so requests after idle periods do not pay a cold start.

option_breakdown.A: Tagging a revision without traffic validates a release before exposing it; it is not how you roll back or change scaling.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Setting a minimum number of instances keeps containers warm so requests after idle periods do not pay a cold start.
option_breakdown.C: Traffic splitting distributes requests across existing revisions; it does not deploy new code or change concurrency.
option_breakdown.D: Rolling back re-points traffic at an older revision; it does not create a canary or change resource settings.

questions.title: Pod stuck in Pending
questions.summary: The Events section of describe reports scheduling failures such as insufficient CPU.
questions.question: A Pod has been stuck in Pending for ten minutes and you need to know why the scheduler will not place it. Which command should you run?

options.A: Run kubectl scale deployment.
options.B: Run kubectl describe pod.
options.C: Run kubectl set image deployment.
options.D: Run kubectl rollout undo deployment.

explanation.summary: The Events section of kubectl describe pod reports scheduling failures such as insufficient CPU or unsatisfied node affinity.

option_breakdown.A: scale changes the replica count; it neither inspects state nor updates the image.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The Events section of kubectl describe pod reports scheduling failures such as insufficient CPU or unsatisfied node affinity.
option_breakdown.C: set image triggers a rolling update to a new container image; it does not scale or inspect.
option_breakdown.D: rollout undo reverts a Deployment to its previous ReplicaSet; it is a rollback, not a deployment or an inspection.

questions.title: Stack trace from a crash-looping container
questions.summary: kubectl logs --previous prints output from the terminated container instance.
questions.question: A container is restarting repeatedly and you need to see the stack trace it printed just before it died. Which command should you run?

options.A: Run kubectl rollout undo deployment.
options.B: Run gcloud container clusters get-credentials.
options.C: Run kubectl logs.
options.D: Run kubectl describe pod.

explanation.summary: kubectl logs --previous prints the output of the terminated container instance, which is where the fatal stack trace is.

option_breakdown.A: rollout undo reverts a Deployment to its previous ReplicaSet; it is a rollback, not a deployment or an inspection.
option_breakdown.B: This fetches cluster credentials into kubeconfig; it inspects nothing and changes no workload.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. kubectl logs --previous prints the output of the terminated container instance, which is where the fatal stack trace is.
option_breakdown.D: describe shows configuration and recent events, which diagnoses scheduling problems but shows no application output.

questions.title: Roll out a patched image to a Deployment
questions.summary: kubectl set image updates the pod template, triggering a native rolling update.
questions.question: A patched image must be rolled out to a running Deployment without editing and reapplying the manifest by hand. Which command should you run?

options.A: Run kubectl describe pod.
options.B: Run kubectl logs.
options.C: Run kubectl scale deployment.
options.D: Run kubectl set image deployment.

explanation.summary: kubectl set image updates the Deployment's pod template, which triggers Kubernetes' native rolling update.

option_breakdown.A: describe shows configuration and recent events, which diagnoses scheduling problems but shows no application output.
option_breakdown.B: logs prints a container's stdout and stderr; it reveals nothing about why a Pod failed to be scheduled.
option_breakdown.C: scale changes the replica count; it neither inspects state nor updates the image.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. kubectl set image updates the Deployment's pod template, which triggers Kubernetes' native rolling update.

explanation.gcloud_command: kubectl set image deployment/api api=us-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/repo/api:v2 -n prod

questions.title: Restore the previous Deployment version
questions.summary: kubectl rollout undo re-points the Deployment at its previous ReplicaSet.
questions.question: The image just rolled out is crash-looping and the previous version must be restored immediately, without rebuilding anything. Which command should you run?

options.A: Run kubectl rollout undo deployment.
options.B: Run kubectl scale deployment.
options.C: Run kubectl set image deployment.
options.D: Run gcloud container clusters get-credentials.

explanation.summary: kubectl rollout undo re-points the Deployment at the previous ReplicaSet, which is the fastest restoration path.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. kubectl rollout undo re-points the Deployment at the previous ReplicaSet, which is the fastest restoration path.
option_breakdown.B: scale changes the replica count; it neither inspects state nor updates the image.
option_breakdown.C: set image triggers a rolling update to a new container image; it does not scale or inspect.
option_breakdown.D: This fetches cluster credentials into kubeconfig; it inspects nothing and changes no workload.

questions.summary: kubectl scale sets the Deployment replica count directly.
questions.question: A predictable traffic surge is expected in an hour and the replica count must be raised ahead of it rather than reactively. Which command should you run?

options.A: Run gcloud container clusters get-credentials.
options.B: Run kubectl scale deployment.
options.C: Run kubectl describe pod.
options.D: Run kubectl logs.

explanation.summary: kubectl scale sets the Deployment's replica count directly, which is how you pre-provision for a known surge.

option_breakdown.A: This fetches cluster credentials into kubeconfig; it inspects nothing and changes no workload.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. kubectl scale sets the Deployment's replica count directly, which is how you pre-provision for a known surge.
option_breakdown.C: describe shows configuration and recent events, which diagnoses scheduling problems but shows no application output.
option_breakdown.D: logs prints a container's stdout and stderr; it reveals nothing about why a Pod failed to be scheduled.

questions.title: ImagePullBackOff on GKE nodes
questions.summary: Image pulls use the node pool's service account, which needs Artifact Registry Reader.
questions.question: GKE Pods fail to start with ImagePullBackOff. You confirm the image exists and that the node service account has no Artifact Registry permissions. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the Artifact Registry Writer role to the build service account.
options.B: Run gcloud auth configure-docker for the registry host.
options.C: Grant the Artifact Registry Reader role to the node pool's service account.
options.D: Create an Artifact Registry repository in the required region and format.

explanation.summary: GKE nodes pull images with the node pool's service account, not the Pod's Workload Identity. Grant that service account Artifact Registry Reader on the repository.

option_breakdown.A: Writer permits pushing images; granting it to a runtime workload that only pulls violates least privilege.
option_breakdown.B: Configuring the Docker credential helper solves local client authentication; it grants no IAM permission.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Image pulls are made by the kubelet with the node pool's service account, so that identity needs roles/artifactregistry.reader on the repository (or project).
option_breakdown.D: Creating a repository is a prerequisite for storing artifacts; it resolves no permission or authentication failure.

questions.title: Cloud Build cannot push the image
questions.summary: Pushing requires Artifact Registry Writer on the target repository for the build identity.
questions.question: A Cloud Build pipeline builds successfully but fails with a permission error when pushing the resulting image to Artifact Registry. What should you do?

options.A: Create an Artifact Registry repository in the required region and format.
options.B: Configure a cleanup policy on the repository.
options.C: Grant the Artifact Registry Reader role to the workload's service account.
options.D: Grant the Artifact Registry Writer role to the build service account.

explanation.summary: Pushing requires the Artifact Registry Writer role on the target repository for the build's service account.

option_breakdown.A: Creating a repository is a prerequisite for storing artifacts; it resolves no permission or authentication failure.
option_breakdown.B: Cleanup policies delete old versions to control storage cost; they have no effect on access.
option_breakdown.C: Reader permits pulling images; it does not allow pushing and does not configure a client's credential helper.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Pushing requires the Artifact Registry Writer role on the target repository for the build's service account.

questions.summary: The Docker client needs the gcloud credential helper registered for the registry host.
questions.question: A developer's local docker push to Artifact Registry is rejected as unauthenticated, even though their gcloud account already holds the Writer role on the repository. What should they do?

options.A: Run gcloud auth configure-docker for the registry host.
options.B: Grant the Artifact Registry Reader role to the workload's service account.
options.C: Grant the Artifact Registry Writer role to the build service account.
options.D: Create an Artifact Registry repository in the required region and format.

explanation.summary: The Docker client needs the gcloud credential helper registered for the registry host before it can present the user's credentials.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The Docker client needs the gcloud credential helper registered for the registry host before it can present the user's credentials.
option_breakdown.B: Reader permits pulling images; it does not allow pushing and does not configure a client's credential helper.
option_breakdown.C: Writer permits pushing images; granting it to a runtime workload that only pulls violates least privilege.
option_breakdown.D: Creating a repository is a prerequisite for storing artifacts; it resolves no permission or authentication failure.

questions.summary: A repository with the right format and location must exist before any push.
questions.question: The team is moving its images off the retired Container Registry (gcr.io) and needs a destination for their Docker images located close to their GKE cluster. What should they do first?

options.B: Create an Artifact Registry repository in the required region and format.

options.D: Grant the Artifact Registry Reader role to the workload's service account.

explanation.summary: An Artifact Registry repository must exist, with the correct format and location, before any image can be pushed to it.

option_breakdown.A: Configuring the Docker credential helper solves local client authentication; it grants no IAM permission.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. An Artifact Registry repository must exist, with the correct format and location, before any image can be pushed to it.
option_breakdown.C: Cleanup policies delete old versions to control storage cost; they have no effect on access.
option_breakdown.D: Reader permits pulling images; it does not allow pushing and does not configure a client's credential helper.

questions.title: Registry storage growing without bound
questions.summary: A cleanup policy deletes versions matching age or count rules automatically.
questions.question: Registry storage costs have grown steadily because every CI run pushes a new tag and nothing is ever deleted. What should you configure?

options.A: Grant the Artifact Registry Reader role to the workload's service account.

options.C: Configure a cleanup policy on the repository.
options.D: Run gcloud auth configure-docker for the registry host.

option_breakdown.B: Writer permits pushing images; granting it to a runtime workload that only pulls violates least privilege.

option_breakdown.D: Configuring the Docker credential helper solves local client authentication; it grants no IAM permission.

questions.title: Add replicas when CPU exceeds 65 percent
questions.summary: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler scales replica count against a target metric.
questions.question: A web Deployment must add replicas when average CPU across its Pods exceeds 65%, and remove them when load falls. What should you configure?

options.A: Configure a VerticalPodAutoscaler.
options.B: Enable cluster autoscaling on the node pool.
options.C: Create an additional node pool with the required machine configuration.
options.D: Configure a HorizontalPodAutoscaler.

explanation.summary: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler scales replica count against a target metric such as average CPU utilisation.

option_breakdown.A: The VPA adjusts each Pod's CPU and memory requests; it does not change the replica count.
option_breakdown.B: Cluster autoscaling adds and removes nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled; it changes no workload's replicas or requests.
option_breakdown.C: A new node pool changes the hardware available; it is not an autoscaling mechanism.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The HorizontalPodAutoscaler scales replica count against a target metric such as average CPU utilisation.

questions.title: Pods Pending because the pool is full
questions.summary: Cluster autoscaling adds nodes when Pods cannot schedule and removes underused ones.
questions.question: Pods are stuck Pending because the node pool has no spare capacity. The team wants nodes added when needed and removed when idle, automatically. What should you configure?

options.A: Enable cluster autoscaling on the node pool.
options.B: Create an additional node pool with the required machine configuration.
options.C: Set explicit CPU and memory resource requests on the Pods.
options.D: Configure a HorizontalPodAutoscaler.

explanation.summary: Cluster autoscaling adds nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled and removes them when they are underused, which is precisely this symptom.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Cluster autoscaling adds nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled and removes them when they are underused, which is precisely this symptom.
option_breakdown.B: A new node pool changes the hardware available; it is not an autoscaling mechanism.
option_breakdown.C: Resource requests determine scheduling and, in Autopilot, billing; they are not themselves an autoscaler.
option_breakdown.D: The HPA changes the number of Pod replicas in response to a metric; it does not resize individual Pods or add nodes.

questions.title: Requests far higher than real usage
questions.summary: The VerticalPodAutoscaler observes real usage and adjusts requests to match.
questions.question: A workload's memory requests were guessed at deployment time and are consistently far above actual usage, wasting cluster capacity. What should you configure?

options.A: Configure a HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
options.B: Configure a VerticalPodAutoscaler.
options.C: Enable cluster autoscaling on the node pool.
options.D: Create an additional node pool with the required machine configuration.

explanation.summary: The VerticalPodAutoscaler observes real usage and adjusts requests to match, which is the remedy for mis-sized requests.

option_breakdown.A: The HPA changes the number of Pod replicas in response to a metric; it does not resize individual Pods or add nodes.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The VerticalPodAutoscaler observes real usage and adjusts requests to match, which is the remedy for mis-sized requests.
option_breakdown.C: Cluster autoscaling adds and removes nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled; it changes no workload's replicas or requests.
option_breakdown.D: A new node pool changes the hardware available; it is not an autoscaling mechanism.

explanation.gcloud_command: kubectl apply -f vpa.yaml   # kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler, updateMode: Auto

questions.title: Controlling Autopilot cost per Pod
questions.summary: Autopilot bills on requested resources, so accurate requests are the direct cost lever.
questions.question: On an Autopilot cluster the team is surprised by the bill and wants a direct lever on what they are charged for each Pod. What should they configure?

options.A: Enable cluster autoscaling on the node pool.
options.B: Create an additional node pool with the required machine configuration.
options.C: Set explicit CPU and memory resource requests on the Pods.
options.D: Configure a HorizontalPodAutoscaler.

explanation.summary: Autopilot bills on the resources a Pod requests, so setting accurate requests is the direct lever on cost.

option_breakdown.A: Autopilot has no node pools for you to autoscale; Google provisions nodes to fit what Pods request, and you are not billed per node.
option_breakdown.B: Node pools are a GKE Standard concept; on Autopilot you do not create them, and you pay for Pod requests, not for machines.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Autopilot bills on the resources a Pod requests, so setting accurate requests is the direct lever on cost.
option_breakdown.D: The HPA changes the number of Pod replicas in response to a metric; it does not resize individual Pods or add nodes.

questions.title: Local SSD cannot be added in place
questions.summary: Node pool hardware properties are fixed at creation, so new hardware means a new pool.
questions.question: A subset of workloads needs nodes with local SSD, and the existing nodes cannot be reconfigured in place to provide it. What should you do?

options.A: Configure a HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
options.B: Configure a VerticalPodAutoscaler.
options.C: Enable cluster autoscaling on the node pool.
options.D: Create an additional node pool with the required machine configuration.

explanation.summary: Node pool properties such as local SSD are fixed at creation, so a new node pool is the only way to introduce different node hardware.

option_breakdown.A: The HPA changes the number of Pod replicas in response to a metric; it does not resize individual Pods or add nodes.
option_breakdown.B: The VPA adjusts each Pod's CPU and memory requests; it does not change the replica count.
option_breakdown.C: Cluster autoscaling adds and removes nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled; it changes no workload's replicas or requests.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Node pool properties such as local SSD are fixed at creation, so a new node pool is the only way to introduce different node hardware.

questions.title: Golden hardened base for every new VM
questions.summary: A custom image bakes the configuration into a bootable template.
questions.question: A hardened, fully patched configuration must be the starting point for every new instance the team creates, so that instances are identical from first boot. What should you create?

options.A: Create a custom image from the configured disk.
options.B: Create a Persistent Disk snapshot.
options.C: Attach a snapshot schedule resource policy to the disk.
options.D: Supply a startup script through instance metadata.

explanation.summary: A custom image bakes the configuration into a bootable template, so every instance created from it starts identical and already hardened.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A custom image bakes the configuration into a bootable template, so every instance created from it starts identical and already hardened.
option_breakdown.B: Snapshots are incremental point-in-time backups of a disk's data; they are not the artefact you deploy new instances from at scale.
option_breakdown.C: A snapshot schedule automates recurring backups; it creates no deployable template and restores nothing by itself.
option_breakdown.D: A startup script configures an instance at boot; it does not capture or restore disk state.

questions.title: Six-hourly backups retained two weeks
questions.summary: A snapshot schedule resource policy performs and expires snapshots automatically.
questions.question: A database disk must be backed up every six hours with backups retained for fourteen days, without anyone remembering to run it. What should you configure?

options.A: Supply a startup script through instance metadata.
options.B: Attach a snapshot schedule resource policy to the disk.
options.C: Create an instance template.
options.D: Create a Persistent Disk snapshot.

explanation.summary: A resource policy snapshot schedule attached to the disk performs and expires the snapshots automatically on the stated cadence and retention.

option_breakdown.A: A startup script configures an instance at boot; it does not capture or restore disk state.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A resource policy snapshot schedule attached to the disk performs and expires the snapshots automatically on the stated cadence and retention.
option_breakdown.C: An instance template captures machine type, disks and metadata for a managed instance group; it does not itself store a disk's contents.
option_breakdown.D: Snapshots are incremental point-in-time backups of a disk's data; they are not the artefact you deploy new instances from at scale.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute resource-policies create snapshot-schedule db-6h --region=us-central1 \
  --max-retention-days=14 --hourly-schedule=6 --start-time=00:00

questions.title: Safety copy before a risky upgrade
questions.summary: A snapshot captures disk state at that moment and can be restored to a new disk.
questions.question: Before a risky in-place upgrade, the engineer needs a point-in-time copy of the data disk that can be restored if the upgrade fails. What should they create?

options.A: Create a custom image from the configured disk.
options.B: Attach a snapshot schedule resource policy to the disk.
options.C: Create a Persistent Disk snapshot.
options.D: Supply a startup script through instance metadata.

explanation.summary: A snapshot captures the disk's state at that moment and can be restored to a new disk, which is the standard pre-change safety step.

option_breakdown.A: Images are the immutable template used to boot new instances; they are not an incremental backup mechanism.
option_breakdown.B: A snapshot schedule automates recurring backups; it creates no deployable template and restores nothing by itself.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A snapshot captures the disk's state at that moment and can be restored to a new disk, which is the standard pre-change safety step.
option_breakdown.D: A startup script configures an instance at boot; it does not capture or restore disk state.

questions.title: SSH without public IPs or a bastion
questions.summary: IAP TCP forwarding tunnels SSH through Google's frontend to the internal address.
questions.question: Instances have no external IP addresses by organisational policy, yet administrators must still open SSH sessions to them, and the team does not want to run a bastion. What should you do?

options.A: Deploy a bastion host with an external IP and connect through it.
options.B: Enable interactive access to the serial console.
options.C: Connect through Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding.
options.D: Enable OS Login and grant the appropriate OS Login IAM role.

explanation.summary: IAP TCP forwarding tunnels the SSH session through Google's frontend to the instance's internal address, so no public IP or bastion is needed.

option_breakdown.A: A bastion works but adds a VM to patch, monitor and secure — unnecessary when IAP provides the same reachability as a managed service.
option_breakdown.B: The serial console recovers an instance whose network stack or sshd is broken; it is not a routine administrative path.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. IAP TCP forwarding tunnels the SSH session through Google's frontend to the instance's internal address, so no public IP or bastion is needed.
option_breakdown.D: OS Login ties Linux accounts to IAM identities and centralises key management; it is not by itself a network path to an instance without a public address.

questions.title: Instance unreachable after a network change
questions.summary: The serial console works independently of the guest network stack.
questions.question: An instance is unreachable over SSH after a misconfigured network change, and the team must get a console prompt to repair the configuration. What should you do?

options.A: Enable OS Login and grant the appropriate OS Login IAM role.
options.B: Connect through Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding.
options.C: Add SSH public keys to project or instance metadata.
options.D: Enable interactive access to the serial console.

explanation.summary: The interactive serial console works independently of the guest network stack, which is why it is the recovery path for exactly this failure.

option_breakdown.A: OS Login ties Linux accounts to IAM identities and centralises key management; it is not by itself a network path to an instance without a public address.
option_breakdown.B: IAP TCP forwarding provides the network path to instances without external IPs; it does not manage Linux user accounts or keys.
option_breakdown.C: Metadata keys are the legacy per-instance mechanism; they scale poorly and are not revoked when someone leaves the organisation.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The interactive serial console works independently of the guest network stack, which is why it is the recovery path for exactly this failure.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instances add-metadata app-1 --zone=us-central1-a \
  --metadata=serial-port-enable=TRUE
gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port app-1 --zone=us-central1-a

questions.title: RDP to a Windows VM without a public IP
questions.summary: IAP TCP forwarding tunnels arbitrary TCP ports, including RDP's 3389.
questions.question: A Windows instance with no external IP must be reachable over RDP by a small group of administrators. What should you do?

options.A: gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel on port 3389, with a firewall rule allowing 35.235.240.0/20 and roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor for the administrators.
options.B: Enable OS Login on the Windows instance.

questions.title: Disable the key to render data unreadable
questions.summary: CMEK puts key lifecycle under your control, so disabling it makes protected data unreadable.
questions.question: Policy requires that the organisation be able to disable the key protecting a BigQuery dataset, rendering the data unreadable on demand. What should you configure?

options.A: Rely on Google-managed encryption keys, applied by default.
options.B: Configure customer-managed encryption keys in Cloud KMS.
options.C: Supply customer-supplied encryption keys with each API request.
options.D: Use a Cloud KMS key with the HSM protection level.

explanation.summary: CMEK puts the key lifecycle under your control, so disabling or destroying the key makes the protected data unreadable — something Google-managed keys cannot offer.

option_breakdown.A: Default encryption at rest is always on and needs no configuration, but gives the customer no control over rotation and no way to revoke access by disabling a key.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. CMEK puts the key lifecycle under your control, so disabling or destroying the key makes the protected data unreadable — something Google-managed keys cannot offer.
option_breakdown.C: CSEK requires passing raw key material on every call and managing it entirely yourself; Google stores nothing, so a lost key means lost data.
option_breakdown.D: An HSM-protected key is generated and used inside a FIPS 140-2 Level 3 module; it costs more than a software key and is required only where that assurance is mandated.

questions.title: FIPS 140-2 Level 3 key material
questions.summary: The HSM protection level in Cloud KMS meets that certification requirement.
questions.question: A regulator requires that key material be generated and used only inside a FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware security module. What should you configure?

options.D: Rely on Google-managed encryption keys, applied by default.

explanation.summary: The HSM protection level in Cloud KMS meets that certification requirement, which software-protected keys do not.

option_breakdown.A: CSEK requires passing raw key material on every call and managing it entirely yourself; Google stores nothing, so a lost key means lost data.
option_breakdown.B: Secret Manager stores and versions application secrets such as passwords and API keys; it does not encrypt storage or database resources.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The HSM protection level in Cloud KMS meets that certification requirement, which software-protected keys do not.
option_breakdown.D: Default encryption at rest is always on and needs no configuration, but gives the customer no control over rotation and no way to revoke access by disabling a key.

options.C: Supply customer-supplied encryption keys with each API request.

questions.title: An Autopilot Pod killed for memory
questions.summary: Autopilot provisions capacity from each container's requests; raise the memory request to give the Pod more.
questions.question: A container on a GKE Autopilot cluster is repeatedly OOMKilled. Its manifest sets a memory request of 512Mi and no other resource values. The application genuinely needs about 1.5 GiB. What should you change?

options.A: Add a node pool with larger machines to the cluster.
options.B: Remove the memory request so Autopilot can allocate memory dynamically.
options.C: Enable the cluster autoscaler on the Autopilot cluster.
options.D: Raise the container's memory request to about 1.5Gi.

explanation.summary: Autopilot sizes capacity, and bills, from Pod resource requests, and applies limits based on them. The fix is a request that matches real usage. Node pools and the cluster autoscaler are managed by Google in Autopilot.

option_breakdown.A: Autopilot manages nodes; you do not add node pools.
option_breakdown.B: Without a request Autopilot applies a small default, which makes the problem worse.
option_breakdown.C: Node scaling is automatic in Autopilot and is not the constraint here.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The request is what Autopilot allocates and bills.

questions.title: A canary split for a Cloud Run function
questions.summary: Cloud Run functions are Cloud Run services, so traffic is split between their revisions with update-traffic.
questions.question: A function deployed with `gcloud functions deploy` (Cloud Run functions) has a new version. You want 20% of requests to reach the new revision and 80% the previous one. What should you do?

options.A: Deploy the new version as a second function and weight the two URLs in Cloud DNS.
options.B: Put both versions behind an external Application Load Balancer with weighted backends.
options.C: Delete the old revision so the platform shifts traffic gradually by itself.
options.D: Split traffic between the function's revisions with `gcloud run services update-traffic`.

explanation.summary: A Cloud Run function is deployed as a Cloud Run service, so it has revisions and supports percentage traffic splits and tags exactly like any other Cloud Run service.

option_breakdown.A: DNS weighting is coarse, cached by clients, and doubles what you operate.
option_breakdown.B: A load balancer is unnecessary; the service already splits traffic between revisions.
option_breakdown.C: Deleting the previous revision removes the rollback target and does not create a gradual split.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Revision-level percentages on the underlying Cloud Run service.

questions.title: Weighted routing between two versions on GKE
questions.summary: With the Gateway API, an HTTPRoute's backendRefs weights split traffic between Services.
questions.question: On GKE, version 1 and version 2 of an application run as separate Deployments, each behind its own Service, exposed through the Gateway API. You want 90% of requests on v1 and 10% on v2. What should you change?

options.A: Scale v1 to nine replicas and v2 to one, relying on one Service selecting both.
options.B: Set the weights in the HTTPRoute's backendRefs: 90 for the v1 Service and 10 for the v2 Service.
options.C: Create a second Gateway for v2 and give users its IP address.
options.D: Add a HorizontalPodAutoscaler to v2 with a 10% CPU target.

explanation.summary: An HTTPRoute can reference several backend Services with weights, and GKE's Gateway controller programs the load balancer to split traffic accordingly — independent of replica counts.

option_breakdown.A: Replica ratios give only approximate splits and couple capacity to routing.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Precise, declarative weights at the load balancer.
option_breakdown.C: A separate entry point means clients choose the version, not a percentage split.
option_breakdown.D: An autoscaler changes replica counts; it does not route traffic.

explanation.gcloud_command: kubectl apply -f route.yaml   # HTTPRoute backendRefs: [{name: app-v1, weight: 90}, {name: app-v2, weight: 10}]

questions.title: Adding a GPU to an existing VM
questions.summary: Attaching a GPU requires the VM to be stopped, host maintenance set to TERMINATE, and the GPU offered in its zone.
questions.question: An existing N1 VM needs an NVIDIA T4 attached for an inference workload. What must be true for the change to succeed?

options.A: The VM is stopped, its host maintenance policy is set to terminate, and T4s are available in its zone.
options.B: The VM keeps running; GPUs are hot-plugged and the maintenance policy is unchanged.
options.C: The VM is converted to a Spot VM, because GPUs are available only on Spot capacity.
options.D: The VM is recreated from a machine image in any region, since GPUs are global resources.

explanation.summary: GPUs cannot live-migrate, so an instance with GPUs must use onHostMaintenance=TERMINATE. The accelerator is attached while the VM is stopped, and only GPU models offered in the VM's zone (and compatible with its machine series) can be attached.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. All three conditions apply to attaching a GPU to an existing instance.
option_breakdown.B: GPUs are not hot-plugged, and live migration is not supported for them.
option_breakdown.C: GPUs are available on standard as well as Spot provisioning.
option_breakdown.D: Accelerators are zonal; availability must be checked per zone.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instances stop infer-1 --zone=ZONE
gcloud compute instances set-scheduling infer-1 --zone=ZONE --maintenance-policy=TERMINATE
gcloud compute instances set-machine-type ...   # or edit the instance to add the accelerator, then start

questions.title: Running a training Pod on TPUs in GKE

option_breakdown.B: CPU requests never cause TPU scheduling.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A TPU node pool plus a google.com/tpu request.
option_breakdown.D: TPUs exist only on TPU machine types; drivers alone do not create hardware.

questions.title: Least privilege for a deployed agent's tools
questions.summary: An agent on Agent Runtime acts through its service identity; grant that identity only the roles its tools need.
questions.question: An agent deployed to Agent Runtime has a tool that queries one BigQuery dataset. It fails with a permission error. The agent must not be able to touch any other data. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the agent's service identity BigQuery Data Viewer on that dataset and BigQuery Job User on the project where it runs queries.
options.B: Grant roles/editor to the agent's service identity so every tool works.
options.C: Embed a service account key with BigQuery Admin in the agent's code.
options.D: Grant BigQuery Data Viewer on the dataset to every user who chats with the agent.

explanation.summary: Agent Runtime runs each agent with a service identity, and every tool call is authorised as that identity. Least privilege means binding exactly the data-read role on the dataset and the job-creation role needed to run queries.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Exactly the permissions the tool needs, on the narrowest scope.
option_breakdown.B: Editor spans every service and makes any prompt injection far more damaging.
option_breakdown.C: Keys are long-lived secrets and unnecessary when the runtime provides an identity.
option_breakdown.D: Tool calls do not run as the chatting user, and this grants data to many people.

questions.title: Finding the slow step inside an agent's answer

options.C: Personalized Service Health for the Agent Platform service.

options.C: gcloud compute zones list --filter='instances>0'
options.D: gcloud compute instances list --filter='status=RUNNING' --format='table(name,zone,machineType)'

explanation.summary: instances list already spans every zone unless restricted. --filter selects on any field, and --format chooses the columns.

option_breakdown.A: describe shows one named instance; it has no --all or --status flags.
option_breakdown.B: There is no --running flag, and ALL is not a zone value.
option_breakdown.C: Zones do not carry an instance count.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Filtered and formatted across all zones.

questions.title: Reading recent rows from Bigtable by key prefix
questions.summary: cbt read with a prefix reads rows whose keys start with a device ID.
questions.question: Bigtable row keys have the form `deviceId#reverseTimestamp`. You need to inspect the most recent five rows for device `pump-17` from the command line. What should you run?

options.A: `cbt -instance=iot read telemetry prefix=pump-17# count=5`
options.B: `bq query 'SELECT * FROM telemetry WHERE device = "pump-17" LIMIT 5'`
options.C: `gcloud bigtable instances describe iot --filter=pump-17`
options.D: `gcloud spanner databases execute-sql telemetry --sql="SELECT * LIMIT 5"`

explanation.summary: cbt is Bigtable's command-line tool. Reading with a key prefix scans only that device's rows, and because the timestamp is reversed, the first rows returned are the newest.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A prefix read, newest first thanks to the reversed timestamp.
option_breakdown.B: BigQuery does not query Bigtable unless an external table is defined, and not with this syntax.
option_breakdown.C: Describing an instance shows its configuration, not table rows.
option_breakdown.D: Spanner commands do not work against Bigtable.

questions.title: An ad-hoc SQL query against a Spanner database
questions.summary: gcloud spanner databases execute-sql runs SQL against a Spanner database from the command line.
questions.question: You need to run a quick SQL query against the `orders` database in the Spanner instance `prod` from Cloud Shell, without installing a client. What should you run?

options.A: `bq query --use_legacy_sql=false 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders'`
options.B: `gcloud sql connect prod --database=orders`
options.C: `gcloud spanner databases execute-sql orders --instance=prod --sql='SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders'`
options.D: `cbt -instance=prod count orders`

explanation.summary: execute-sql sends a SQL statement to a Spanner database and prints the result. (The console's Spanner Studio does the same interactively.)

option_breakdown.A: bq targets BigQuery, not Spanner.
option_breakdown.B: gcloud sql connect is for Cloud SQL instances.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Spanner's own command-line query path.
option_breakdown.D: cbt is for Bigtable.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud spanner databases execute-sql orders --instance=prod --sql='SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders'

questions.title: Estimating a storage bill that includes retrieval
questions.summary: The Pricing Calculator models storage, operations and retrieval together for a planned configuration.
questions.question: Before approving a design, finance wants a monthly estimate for keeping 200 TB in Coldline Storage, of which about 5% is read back each month. Nothing is deployed yet. What should you do?

options.A: Create the bucket, upload a sample, and read the next invoice.
options.B: Model the storage, the operations and the retrieval volume in the Google Cloud Pricing Calculator.
options.C: Multiply 200 TB by the Coldline per-GB storage price and report that figure.
options.D: Create a budget of the expected amount and read its forecast.

explanation.summary: The Pricing Calculator estimates planned resources, including the retrieval fees and operation charges that colder classes add. Counting only the per-GB storage price understates the cost of reading data back.

option_breakdown.A: Deploying first is slow and costly, and a sample does not show the real bill.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Storage, operations and retrieval together, before anything exists.
option_breakdown.C: Coldline charges for retrieval and operations as well; ignoring them understates the estimate.
option_breakdown.D: Budgets forecast from actual spend, and there is no spend yet.

explanation.gcloud_command: # https://cloud.google.com/products/calculator > Cloud Storage > Coldline, 200 TB, retrieval 10 TB/month

questions.title: Scheduled Firestore backups kept for weeks
questions.summary: Firestore backup schedules take daily or weekly backups; restores create a new database.
questions.question: A Firestore database needs a daily backup kept for 14 weeks, and the team must be able to restore any of those backups without affecting the live database. What should you configure?

options.A: Point-in-time recovery, which keeps versions for 14 weeks.
options.B: A nightly export from the application into a bucket it also serves traffic from.
options.C: Firestore in multi-region mode, which keeps historical copies automatically.
options.D: A Firestore backup schedule with daily recurrence and 14-week retention; restore into a new database.

explanation.summary: Firestore scheduled backups run daily or weekly with a retention of up to 14 weeks. A restore always creates a new database from the backup, leaving the live one untouched.

option_breakdown.A: Point-in-time recovery covers a short recent window (about seven days), not 14 weeks.
option_breakdown.B: Application-driven exports are fragile and mix backup files with serving data.
option_breakdown.C: Multi-region replication provides availability, not history.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Managed schedule, managed retention, restore to a new database.

questions.title: Recovering an AlloyDB cluster to ten minutes ago
questions.summary: AlloyDB continuous backup allows point-in-time recovery into a new cluster.
questions.question: A bad deployment corrupted data in an AlloyDB for PostgreSQL cluster ten minutes ago. Continuous backup and recovery is enabled with its default settings. How do you get the data as it was just before the deployment?

options.A: Restore from continuous backup to a point in time just before the deployment, into a new cluster.
options.B: Promote the read pool instance, which lags the primary by ten minutes.
options.C: Restore last night's on-demand backup over the running cluster.
options.D: Export the database and remove the corrupted rows by hand.

explanation.summary: Continuous backup keeps the logs needed to recover to any point in its retention window. Point-in-time recovery creates a new cluster at the chosen timestamp, which you then validate and switch to.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Point-in-time recovery to the moment before the damage.
option_breakdown.B: Read pools serve reads with very little lag and cannot be promoted as a recovery point.
option_breakdown.C: Last night's backup loses a day of good data, and a restore goes into a new cluster anyway.
option_breakdown.D: Hand-editing an export is error-prone and slow.

questions.title: Why a Dataflow job has stopped making progress
questions.summary: The Dataflow job page shows the job graph, per-stage progress, throughput and worker logs.
questions.question: A streaming Dataflow job's output has stopped updating, although the job still shows as running. You need to see which stage is stuck and the errors its workers are logging. Where should you look?

options.A: The Pub/Sub topic's publish rate chart.
options.B: The job's page in the Dataflow monitoring interface: the job graph, stage metrics and worker logs.
options.C: The Compute Engine VM list, SSHing into each worker in turn.
options.D: BigQuery's INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS view.

explanation.summary: The Dataflow monitoring interface shows each stage of the job graph with its throughput, data freshness and system lag, plus job and worker logs. A stage with growing lag and errors in its logs is the one that is stuck.

option_breakdown.A: Upstream publish rates show input, not where the pipeline is blocked.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Per-stage status and worker errors in one place.
option_breakdown.C: Workers are managed and short-lived; SSH is slow and misses the job-level view.
option_breakdown.D: INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS lists BigQuery jobs, not Dataflow pipelines.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud dataflow jobs describe JOB_ID --region=REGION
gcloud dataflow jobs list --status=active --region=REGION

questions.title: Checking whether a BigQuery job succeeded
questions.summary: bq show -j (or INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS) reports a BigQuery job's state, errors and bytes processed.
questions.question: A nightly load into BigQuery was started by a script that only recorded the job ID. You need to know whether the job finished, and if not, what error it hit. What should you run?

options.A: `bq ls -j` for last week and assume the newest entry is the job.
options.B: `gcloud logging read` for the dataset name, without a filter.
options.C: `bq show -j JOB_ID`
options.D: `bq head` on the destination table to see whether rows arrived.

explanation.summary: bq show -j prints a job's configuration, state (PENDING, RUNNING, DONE) and any error result. For many jobs, INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS answers the same in SQL.

option_breakdown.A: Listing jobs and guessing is unreliable when you already have the ID.
option_breakdown.B: Unfiltered log searches are slow and noisy compared with asking for the job.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. State and error of that exact job.
option_breakdown.D: Row presence says nothing about failure or partial loads.

questions.title: Fleet-wide database risks across many projects
questions.summary: Database Center gives one view of the database fleet across projects and flags issues like missing backups.
questions.question: A company runs about 200 Cloud SQL, AlloyDB and Spanner instances across 60 projects. The security lead wants one place to see which instances have no automated backups, have a public IP, or are not highly available. What should you use?

options.A: Query Insights on each instance.
options.B: A Cloud Monitoring dashboard per project.
options.C: The billing export, grouped by SKU.
options.D: Database Center.

explanation.summary: Database Center is the fleet view for Google Cloud databases: an inventory across projects and engines, with health issues such as missing backups, public IP exposure or lack of high availability, and recommendations to fix them.

option_breakdown.A: Query Insights diagnoses query performance on a single instance.
option_breakdown.B: Per-project dashboards show metrics, not configuration risks across the fleet.
option_breakdown.C: Billing rows do not describe backup or network configuration.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. One inventory with the health issues surfaced.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Database Center (filter by issue: no automated backups, public IP, not HA)

questions.title: Database engine versions nearing end of support
questions.summary: Database Center shows engine versions across the fleet, so outdated versions are found in one place.
questions.question: A database team must find every database in the organisation still running an engine version that is approaching end of support, across Cloud SQL, AlloyDB and Spanner, to plan upgrades. What should they use?

options.A: Database Center, filtering the fleet inventory by engine version.
options.B: Query Insights, sorting queries by average latency.
options.C: gcloud sql instances list in each project, copied into a spreadsheet.
options.D: Personalized Service Health.

explanation.summary: Database Center presents the whole database fleet — engine, version, location, project — and surfaces version-related issues, so the upgrade backlog comes from one filtered view.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Fleet-wide inventory including engine versions.
option_breakdown.B: Query Insights is about query performance, not versions.
option_breakdown.C: Per-project loops cover only Cloud SQL and go stale immediately.
option_breakdown.D: Service Health reports Google Cloud incidents, not your databases' versions.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Database Center > filter: Engine version

questions.title: CMEK bucket creation fails on key permission
questions.summary: With CMEK, the service's Google-managed service agent needs Encrypter/Decrypter on the Cloud KMS key.
questions.question: Creating a Cloud Storage bucket with a default customer-managed encryption key fails with a permission error on the key, although you are an Owner of both the project and the key's project. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the project's Cloud Storage service agent the Cloud KMS CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter role on the key.
options.B: Grant yourself Cloud KMS Admin on the key ring.
options.C: Create the key in the same bucket location with the HSM protection level.
options.D: Switch to customer-supplied encryption keys, which need no IAM grant.

explanation.summary: Cloud Storage encrypts and decrypts with the key on your behalf through its service agent (service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gs-project-accounts.iam.gserviceaccount.com). That identity — not you — needs roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter on the key.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The service agent performs the cryptographic operations and needs the role.
option_breakdown.B: Your own permissions are not what the storage service uses.
option_breakdown.C: Protection level does not change who may use the key.
option_breakdown.D: CSEK is a different model with its own drawbacks and does not fix the missing grant.

questions.title: A route to an appliance that drops the traffic
questions.summary: A VM used as a route's next hop must be created with IP forwarding enabled.
questions.question: You add a custom static route sending 172.16.0.0/12 to a firewall appliance VM as its next hop. Packets reach the appliance's interface but are never forwarded onward, although the appliance software is configured correctly. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The route's priority is 1000, which is too low for custom routes.
options.B: Custom static routes do not support instance next hops.
options.C: The appliance VM was created without IP forwarding (canIpForward) enabled.
options.D: The subnet needs Private Google Access for routed traffic.

explanation.summary: By default Compute Engine drops packets whose source or destination is not the VM's own address. A VM that forwards traffic — the next hop of a custom route — must be created with IP forwarding enabled.

option_breakdown.A: 1000 is the default priority and is a valid value for custom routes.
option_breakdown.B: Instances are a supported next-hop type for static routes.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Without IP forwarding the VM will not pass through traffic for other addresses.
option_breakdown.D: Private Google Access concerns reaching Google APIs, not routing to an appliance.

questions.title: Finding shadowed and unused firewall rules
questions.summary: Firewall Insights reports shadowed, overly permissive and unused firewall rules from rule-hit data.
questions.question: A VPC has accumulated 400 firewall rules. You want to find the rules that are shadowed by other rules and those with no hits in the last six weeks, so they can be cleaned up safely. What should you use?

options.A: gcloud compute firewall-rules list sorted by priority, reviewed by hand.
options.B: Firewall Insights in Network Intelligence Center.
options.C: VPC Flow Logs exported to BigQuery for a year.
options.D: The IAM role recommender.

explanation.summary: Firewall Insights analyses configuration and firewall-rule hit counts to report shadowed rules, overly permissive rules and rules with no recent hits.

option_breakdown.A: Manual review of 400 rules misses shadowing that depends on overlapping ranges and targets.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Built for this analysis of firewall rules.
option_breakdown.C: Flow logs record connections, not which rule allowed them, and cost more.
option_breakdown.D: The role recommender reduces IAM grants, not firewall rules.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Network Intelligence Center > Firewall Insights

questions.title: Switching a firewall rule off without losing it
questions.summary: A VPC firewall rule can be disabled and re-enabled in place with --disabled / --no-disabled.
questions.question: To test whether a specific allow rule is responsible for some traffic, you want to switch it off for an hour and then restore it exactly as it was. What should you do?

options.A: Delete the rule and recreate it from memory afterwards.
options.B: Change its source range to 0.0.0.0/32 and change it back later.
options.C: Raise its priority number to 65535.
options.D: Update the rule with --disabled, then re-enable it with --no-disabled.

explanation.summary: A disabled rule stays in the configuration with all its settings but is not enforced; re-enabling it restores the original behaviour exactly.

option_breakdown.A: Recreating from memory risks changing the rule.
option_breakdown.B: Editing ranges is a change to remember and reverse, not a toggle.
option_breakdown.C: An allow rule at 65535 still allows traffic that no other rule decides.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A clean, reversible toggle.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute firewall-rules update allow-web --disabled
gcloud compute firewall-rules update allow-web --no-disabled

questions.title: A business metric emitted by the application
questions.summary: Applications write custom metrics to Cloud Monitoring through OpenTelemetry or the Monitoring API.
questions.question: A Cloud Run service knows how many orders are waiting for fraud review. Operations wants that number charted and alerted on in Cloud Monitoring, sampled every minute. What should you do?

options.A: Log the number at INFO level and read it in the Logs Explorer.
options.B: Estimate it from the service's request count metric.
options.C: Instrument the service to write the value as a custom metric (OpenTelemetry or the Monitoring API) and alert on that metric.
options.D: Store the number in a BigQuery table and build a Looker Studio chart.

explanation.summary: Values only the application knows become metrics when the application exports them — through OpenTelemetry with the Google Cloud exporter or directly with the Cloud Monitoring API. They can then be charted and used in alerting policies like any built-in metric.

option_breakdown.A: Reading log lines is not a metric, and alerting would first need a log-based metric.
option_breakdown.B: Request volume does not measure a queue that the application alone tracks.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. An application-emitted metric, alertable like any other.
option_breakdown.D: BigQuery plus a report cannot drive a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy.

explanation.gcloud_command: # OpenTelemetry SDK + Google Cloud Monitoring exporter: gauge 'fraud_review_backlog'

questions.title: Which connections a deny rule blocked
questions.summary: Firewall Rules Logging records the connections a specific rule allowed or denied.
questions.question: An application team says their traffic is being blocked. You suspect one particular deny rule and need a record of the connections it blocks, with source and destination details. What should you enable?

options.A: Data Access audit logs for the Compute Engine API.
options.B: Logging on that firewall rule (Firewall Rules Logging).
options.C: Admin Activity audit logs, which record every packet decision.
options.D: Uptime checks against the application's endpoint.

explanation.summary: Firewall Rules Logging, enabled per rule, writes a log entry for each connection that rule allows or denies, including source, destination, ports and the rule's name.

option_breakdown.A: Data Access logs record API reads, not network traffic.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Per-rule connection records for the suspected rule.
option_breakdown.C: Admin Activity logs record configuration changes, not traffic.
option_breakdown.D: Uptime checks test reachability from outside; they do not say which rule blocked what.

questions.title: Only the errors from one Cloud Run service
questions.summary: The logging query language filters on resource type, labels and severity together.
questions.question: In the Logs Explorer you want to see only entries of severity ERROR or worse from the Cloud Run service named `api`. Which query should you use?

options.A: `api AND ERROR`
options.B: `logName="api" AND severity=ERROR`
options.C: `resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND resource.labels.service_name="api" AND severity>=ERROR`
options.D: `textPayload:"ERROR" AND resource.type="gce_instance"`

explanation.summary: Cloud Run entries carry resource.type cloud_run_revision with the service name as a resource label. Severity is ordered, so >= ERROR includes CRITICAL, ALERT and EMERGENCY.

option_breakdown.A: Free-text terms match anywhere, including other services and messages that merely contain the words.
option_breakdown.B: A log name is not the service name, and = ERROR misses more severe entries.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Resource, service and severity in the query language.
option_breakdown.D: Wrong resource type, and text matching misses structured severities.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND resource.labels.service_name="api" AND severity>=ERROR' --limit=50

questions.title: Who made a call, and from which address
questions.summary: An audit log entry's protoPayload carries the caller's principal and IP address.
questions.question: You have found the audit log entry for a firewall rule being deleted. You now need the identity that made the call and the IP address it came from. Which fields should you read in the entry?

options.A: `resource.labels.project_id` and `timestamp`
options.B: `severity` and `logName`
options.C: `jsonPayload.user` and `httpRequest.remoteIp`
options.D: `protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail` and `protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp`

explanation.summary: Cloud Audit Logs entries use the AuditLog payload. authenticationInfo.principalEmail is the caller, and requestMetadata.callerIp is where the request came from; methodName and resourceName describe what was done.

option_breakdown.A: They identify where and when, not who.
option_breakdown.B: They classify the entry, not the caller.
option_breakdown.C: Audit entries use protoPayload, not jsonPayload, and httpRequest belongs to request logs.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The caller identity and source address of the call.

questions.title: Which index would fix the slow queries
questions.summary: Index advisor in Query Insights recommends indexes for slow queries on Cloud SQL and AlloyDB.
questions.question: Query Insights shows that a few queries on a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance account for most of the load, and they scan large tables. You want recommendations for which indexes to create, with the estimated benefit. What should you use?

options.A: Index advisor in Query Insights.
options.B: Cloud Profiler on the database VM.
options.C: The Compute Engine machine-type recommender.
options.D: Cloud Trace for the application calling the database.

explanation.summary: Index advisor analyses the recorded queries and recommends indexes that would speed them up, with the estimated impact and the CREATE INDEX statements to apply.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Index recommendations from the observed query workload.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud SQL is managed; Profiler instruments your own application code.
option_breakdown.C: Machine-type recommendations resize VMs; they do not address missing indexes.
option_breakdown.D: Trace shows that the database call is slow, not which index would help.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Cloud SQL > instance > Query insights > Index advisor

questions.title: Being told when a Google incident affects your projects
questions.summary: Personalized Service Health can alert through Cloud Monitoring on incidents affecting your projects.
questions.question: On-call wants to be notified automatically when Google Cloud posts an incident that affects Cloud SQL in europe-west1 for the projects they run, rather than checking a public status page. What should you configure?

options.A: An uptime check against the public Google Cloud status page.
options.B: A log-based metric on Cloud SQL error logs.
options.C: An alerting policy on Personalized Service Health events for the relevant product and location.
options.D: A budget alert that fires when Cloud SQL spend changes.

explanation.summary: Personalized Service Health shows Google Cloud incidents relevant to your projects and can drive Cloud Monitoring alerting policies filtered by product, location and relevance.

option_breakdown.A: The public page is not personalised, and polling it is not an integration.
option_breakdown.B: Your own errors may or may not come from a Google incident; this does not report incidents.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Incident notifications scoped to the products and locations you use.
option_breakdown.D: Spend has no relationship to incidents.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Service Health > Configure alerts (product: Cloud SQL, location: europe-west1)

questions.title: One application-centric operations view
questions.summary: Cloud Hub gives an app-centric view of active events, health, deployments and maintenance for App Hub apps.
questions.question: An application team registered their services in App Hub. They want one place, organised by application, that shows active incidents affecting it, upcoming maintenance, recent deployment status and health — rather than switching between product pages. What should they use?

options.A: Cloud Asset Inventory feeds.
options.B: Cloud Hub.
options.C: A Cloud Monitoring metrics scope.
options.D: Query Insights.

explanation.summary: Cloud Hub is the application-centric operations front door: for App Hub applications it brings together active events and incidents, health, deployments, maintenance and related signals.

option_breakdown.A: Asset feeds stream configuration changes; they are not an operations dashboard.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Application-centric events and health in one view.
option_breakdown.C: A metrics scope aggregates metrics across projects but not incidents, maintenance and deployments by application.
option_breakdown.D: Query Insights is limited to database query performance.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Cloud Hub > select the App Hub application

questions.title: AI-assisted root-cause investigation after an alert
questions.summary: Gemini Cloud Assist investigations correlate logs, metrics and recent changes to suggest likely causes.
questions.question: An alert fired for rising error rates on a GKE workload. The on-call engineer wants an AI-assisted analysis that correlates the relevant logs, metrics and recent configuration changes and proposes likely root causes. What should they start?

options.A: Active Assist's idle VM recommender.
options.B: A new uptime check on the workload.
options.C: Cloud Profiler on every Pod.
options.D: A Gemini Cloud Assist investigation from the alert or the affected resource.

explanation.summary: Gemini Cloud Assist investigations gather signals — logs, metrics, recent changes, known issues — around the affected resources and produce hypotheses about the cause, with next steps.

option_breakdown.A: Idle-resource recommendations are about cost, not incidents.
option_breakdown.B: An uptime check would detect the problem again, not explain it.
option_breakdown.C: Profiler shows CPU hot spots; it does not correlate errors with changes.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. An AI-assisted investigation across logs, metrics and changes.

questions.title: Collecting an application's own log file with the Ops Agent
questions.summary: The Ops Agent reads extra log files when you add a files receiver to its config.yaml and restart it.
questions.question: The Ops Agent is running on a VM and sends system logs, but the application's log file at `/var/log/app/app.log` never appears in Cloud Logging. What should you do?

options.A: Add a `files` receiver for that path to a logging pipeline in `/etc/google-cloud-ops-agent/config.yaml` and restart the agent.
options.B: Install the legacy Logging agent alongside the Ops Agent.
options.C: Grant the VM's service account Logs Viewer.
options.D: Move the file to `/var/log/syslog`, the only path the agent can read.

explanation.summary: By default the Ops Agent collects system logs. Other files are added by defining a receiver of type files with their paths, adding it to a pipeline in config.yaml, and restarting the agent.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A files receiver in the agent's configuration.
option_breakdown.B: Running both agents is unsupported and unnecessary.
option_breakdown.C: Writing logs needs Logs Writer, which the default setup already has; Viewer is for reading.
option_breakdown.D: Any path can be configured; moving application logs is not required.

explanation.gcloud_command: sudo systemctl restart google-cloud-ops-agent   # after adding receivers: app: {type: files, include_paths: [...]}

questions.title: Scraping an application's /metrics endpoint on GKE
questions.summary: With managed collection, a PodMonitoring resource tells Managed Service for Prometheus which Pods to scrape.
questions.question: Managed collection for Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus is enabled on a GKE cluster. A new Deployment exposes Prometheus metrics on port 9090 at /metrics, but none of its metrics appear in Cloud Monitoring. What should you add?

options.A: A PodMonitoring resource selecting the Deployment's Pods and the metrics port.
options.B: The Ops Agent, installed on every node through a DaemonSet.
options.C: A self-managed Prometheus server with remote write to BigQuery.
options.D: A log-based metric parsing the /metrics output from container logs.

explanation.summary: Managed collection runs the collectors for you, but scraping is opt-in per workload: a PodMonitoring (or ClusterPodMonitoring) resource names the label selector, port and path to scrape.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. It declares what the managed collectors should scrape.
option_breakdown.B: The Ops Agent is for Compute Engine VMs; GKE uses managed collection for Prometheus metrics.
option_breakdown.C: Running your own server is what the managed service replaces, and BigQuery is not a Prometheus backend.
option_breakdown.D: Metrics are scraped over HTTP, not parsed from logs.

explanation.gcloud_command: kubectl apply -f podmonitoring.yaml   # kind: PodMonitoring, selector app=orders, endpoints: port 9090, path /metrics

questions.title: Which Pods are using the most memory right now
questions.summary: kubectl top pods shows live CPU and memory use per Pod from the metrics server.
questions.question: Nodes in namespace shop are under memory pressure and you want to see, right now, which Pods consume the most memory. Which command gives you that directly?

options.A: kubectl get pods -n shop -o wide
options.B: kubectl describe deployment -n shop
options.C: gcloud container node-pools list --cluster=CLUSTER --location=REGION
options.D: kubectl top pods -n shop --sort-by=memory

explanation.summary: kubectl top reads current resource usage from the cluster's metrics API and can sort Pods by memory.

option_breakdown.A: get -o wide shows Pod status, IP and node, not resource usage.
option_breakdown.B: describe shows a Deployment's spec, replicas and events, not live consumption.
option_breakdown.C: Listing node pools shows their configuration, not what Pods are using.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. kubectl top reads current resource usage from the cluster's metrics API and can sort Pods by memory.

explanation.gcloud_command:
kubectl top pods -n shop --sort-by=memory
kubectl top nodes

questions.title: Moving a node pool to a bigger machine type
questions.summary: Node machine type is fixed per pool: create a new pool, cordon and drain the old one, then delete it.
questions.question: A GKE Standard node pool of e2-standard-4 nodes must move to n2-standard-8 with the least disruption to running workloads. What is the recommended approach?

options.A: Create a new node pool with n2-standard-8, cordon and drain the old pool's nodes, then delete the old pool.
options.B: Edit the machine type of the existing node pool in place.
options.C: Resize the old pool to zero first, then create the new pool.
options.D: Stop each node VM in Compute Engine and change its machine type.

explanation.summary: A node pool's machine type is not editable; a new pool lets Pods reschedule gracefully as the old nodes are drained, before the old pool is removed.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A node pool's machine type is not editable; a new pool lets Pods reschedule gracefully as the old nodes are drained, before the old pool is removed.
option_breakdown.B: The machine type of an existing pool cannot be changed.
option_breakdown.C: Scaling the old pool to zero before the new one exists leaves Pods with nowhere to run.
option_breakdown.D: Nodes are managed by the pool's instance group; editing the VMs is overwritten and unsupported.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud container node-pools create pool-n2 --cluster=C --location=R --machine-type=n2-standard-8
kubectl cordon NODE && kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
gcloud container node-pools delete default-pool --cluster=C --location=R

questions.title: HPA and VPA fighting over CPU
questions.summary: Do not let HPA and VPA act on the same CPU or memory metric; scale HPA on another metric or run VPA in recommendation mode.
questions.question: A Deployment has an HPA targeting 60% CPU and a VPA in Auto mode managing CPU requests. Replica counts and Pod sizes oscillate all day. The team wants horizontal scaling plus right-sized requests. What should it change?

options.A: Scale the HPA on a different metric, such as requests per second, or put the VPA in recommendation-only mode.
options.B: Add a second HPA on memory.
options.C: Raise the HPA's maximum replicas.
options.D: Set both HPA and VPA to target 80% CPU.

explanation.summary: When both autoscalers react to CPU, each change triggers the other; separating their signals — or letting VPA only recommend — stops the loop.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. When both autoscalers react to CPU, each change triggers the other; separating their signals — or letting VPA only recommend — stops the loop.
option_breakdown.B: Another HPA adds a third controller to the same fight.
option_breakdown.C: A higher ceiling lets the oscillation grow larger.
option_breakdown.D: Aligning targets keeps both acting on the same metric.

explanation.gcloud_command:
kubectl autoscale deployment web --min=3 --max=30 --cpu-percent=60   # replace with a custom-metric HPA
# VPA spec: updatePolicy: { updateMode: "Off" }   # recommendations only

questions.title: Cheaper Autopilot Pods for interruptible work
questions.summary: Autopilot runs Pods on Spot capacity when they select cloud.google.com/gke-spot: "true".
questions.question: A nightly batch on GKE Autopilot checkpoints its progress and can be interrupted and restarted. The team wants to pay less for it without leaving Autopilot. What should it change in the Pod spec?

options.A: Create a Spot node pool in the cluster.
options.B: Lower the Pods' CPU requests below Autopilot's minimum.
options.C: Add a PriorityClass with a low priority.
options.D: Add a nodeSelector of cloud.google.com/gke-spot: "true".
