questions.question: A VPC has 120 VPC firewall rules, none using network tags or service accounts. The team wants to manage them as a global network firewall policy without retyping each rule. What should it use?

options.A: gcloud beta compute firewall-rules migrate --source-network=prod --target-firewall-policy=prod-policy, then associate the policy with the network.
options.B: gcloud compute firewall-rules list --format=json, then import the file as an organization policy.
options.C: gcloud compute network-firewall-policies associations create, which converts the rules automatically.
options.D: Delete the VPC firewall rules; a network firewall policy inherits them.

explanation.summary: The migration tool creates a global network firewall policy from the network's VPC firewall rules, keeping their evaluation order. You then associate the policy with the network to activate it.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The migration tool creates a global network firewall policy from the network's VPC firewall rules, keeping their evaluation order. You then associate the policy with the network to activate it.
option_breakdown.B: Organization policies are not firewall policies and cannot hold rules.
option_breakdown.C: Associating a policy only attaches it; it copies no rules.
option_breakdown.D: Deleting the rules removes the protection; nothing is inherited.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud beta compute firewall-rules migrate --source-network=prod --target-firewall-policy=prod-policy
gcloud compute network-firewall-policies associations create --firewall-policy=prod-policy \
  --network=prod --global-firewall-policy

questions.title: Letting projects decide traffic an org policy should not judge
questions.summary: A hierarchical rule with action goto_next passes evaluation down to lower levels.
questions.question: An organization's hierarchical firewall policy denies all ingress from the internet at priority 1000. The networking team wants traffic from the corporate range 203.0.113.0/24 to be decided by each project's own firewall rules rather than allowed or denied at the organization level. Which rule should be added above the deny?

options.A: A rule for 203.0.113.0/24 with the action goto_next.
options.B: A rule for 203.0.113.0/24 with the action allow.
options.C: A rule for 203.0.113.0/24 with the action deny and logging enabled.
options.D: No rule; lower-level rules always override organization rules.

explanation.summary: goto_next stops evaluation at this level and hands the connection to the next level (folder, then the VPC's firewall rules and policies), which then decides.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. goto_next stops evaluation at this level and hands the connection to the next level (folder, then the VPC's firewall rules and policies), which then decides.
option_breakdown.B: allow would permit the traffic everywhere, overriding the projects' decisions.
option_breakdown.C: deny blocks the traffic; logging does not delegate it.
option_breakdown.D: Hierarchical rules are evaluated first, and a matching allow or deny is final.

questions.title: Seeing which connections a policy rule is matching
questions.summary: Enable logging on the specific firewall policy rule to write Firewall Rules Logging entries.
questions.question: A deny rule at priority 2000 in a global network firewall policy may be blocking a partner's traffic. You want records of each connection that the rule matches, with source and destination details. What should you do?

options.A: Enable VPC Flow Logs on the subnet and look for dropped packets.
options.B: Turn on Data Access audit logs for the Compute Engine API.
options.C: Run a Connectivity Test every few minutes.
options.D: Update that policy rule with --enable-logging and view its entries in Cloud Logging.

explanation.summary: Firewall Rules Logging records every connection that a rule with logging enabled allows or denies, including the rule that matched.

option_breakdown.A: Flow Logs sample traffic and do not reliably show the rule that denied it.
option_breakdown.B: Audit logs record API calls, not network connections.
option_breakdown.C: Connectivity Tests analyse configuration for a path you describe; they do not record real traffic.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Firewall Rules Logging records every connection that a rule with logging enabled allows or denies, including the rule that matched.

questions.title: An on-call engineer who cannot see Service Health events
questions.summary: Grant roles/servicehealth.viewer (and enable the Service Health API) for least-privilege access.
questions.question: An on-call engineer has only narrowly scoped custom roles in project shop-prod. They need to view Personalized Service Health events for the project and nothing more. The Service Health API is enabled. What should you grant?

options.A: roles/viewer on shop-prod.
options.B: roles/monitoring.viewer on shop-prod.
options.C: roles/servicehealth.viewer on the billing account.
options.D: roles/servicehealth.viewer on shop-prod.

explanation.summary: The Personalized Service Health Viewer role grants read access to service health events and is the least-privilege choice.

option_breakdown.A: The basic Viewer role would work but grants read access to almost everything in the project.
option_breakdown.B: Monitoring Viewer covers metrics and dashboards, not Service Health events.
option_breakdown.C: Service Health events are scoped to projects and organisations, not billing accounts.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The Personalized Service Health Viewer role grants read access to service health events and is the least-privilege choice.

questions.title: The Gemini Cloud Assist panel will not work in a new project
questions.summary: Enable the Gemini Cloud Assist API and grant users roles/geminicloudassist.user.
questions.question: An SRE team wants to use Gemini Cloud Assist to investigate Cloud Monitoring alerts in a newly created project, but the assistant reports that it is not set up. What must an administrator do?

options.A: Enable geminicloudassist.googleapis.com in the project and grant the SREs roles/geminicloudassist.user.
options.B: Enable the Cloud Monitoring API and grant roles/monitoring.editor.
options.C: Install the Ops Agent on the project's VMs.
options.D: Create a Vertex AI endpoint for Gemini in the project.

explanation.summary: Gemini Cloud Assist needs its API enabled in the project (which also enables the Gemini for Google Cloud API), and users need the Gemini Cloud Assist User role.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Gemini Cloud Assist needs its API enabled in the project (which also enables the Gemini for Google Cloud API), and users need the Gemini Cloud Assist User role.
option_breakdown.B: Monitoring access alone does not enable the assistant.
option_breakdown.C: The Ops Agent collects telemetry; it has nothing to do with setting up Gemini.
option_breakdown.D: Gemini Cloud Assist is a managed console service, not a model you deploy.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud services enable geminicloudassist.googleapis.com --project=PROJECT_ID
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID --member=group:sre@example.com \
  --role=roles/geminicloudassist.user

questions.title: Making sense of a latency spike on a dashboard chart
questions.summary: Gemini Cloud Assist can explain a metric chart or log entry in context and suggest next steps.
questions.question: A junior engineer sees a sudden latency spike on a Cloud Monitoring dashboard chart for a Cloud Run service and does not know which signals to check next. With Gemini Cloud Assist set up, what is the most direct help available?

options.A: Export the metric to BigQuery and run a regression.
options.B: Ask Gemini Cloud Assist about the chart, which explains the spike in context and suggests related metrics and logs to check.
options.C: Open a Google Cloud support case for the chart.
options.D: Create an uptime check on the service's URL.

explanation.summary: Gemini Cloud Assist works inside the console's observability pages. It can explain what a chart or log shows and point to the next data to look at.

option_breakdown.A: Possible, but slow, and it does not explain the spike.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Gemini Cloud Assist works inside the console's observability pages. It can explain what a chart or log shows and point to the next data to look at.
option_breakdown.C: Support is for issues with Google's services, not for reading your own telemetry.
option_breakdown.D: An uptime check measures availability from now on; it does not explain the past spike.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Monitoring > Dashboards > chart > Gemini Cloud Assist (ask about this chart)

questions.title: Why an Autopilot HPA scales out too late
questions.summary: HPA CPU utilisation is measured against requests; oversized requests delay scaling and cost more.
questions.question: On GKE Autopilot, a Deployment requests 2 vCPU per Pod but typically uses 0.3 vCPU. Its HPA targets 70% CPU utilisation and hardly ever adds replicas, even when latency climbs. What is the best fix?

options.A: Raise the HPA target to 95%.
options.B: Raise the CPU request to 4 vCPU.
options.C: Switch the Pods to the Performance compute class.
options.D: Lower the CPU request to near real usage, so both the HPA's utilisation and the Autopilot bill reflect actual use.

explanation.summary: HPA utilisation is usage divided by request. An oversized request makes utilisation look low, so scaling starts late, and on Autopilot you also pay for the unused request.

option_breakdown.A: A higher target makes scaling happen even later.
option_breakdown.B: A bigger request makes the utilisation figure lower still and costs more.
option_breakdown.C: Hardware choice does not fix a mis-sized request.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. HPA utilisation is usage divided by request. An oversized request makes utilisation look low, so scaling starts late, and on Autopilot you also pay for the unused request.

questions.title: Several small inference Pods sharing one GPU
questions.summary: GPU time-sharing lets several containers share one physical GPU on a GKE node.
questions.question: Twelve lightweight inference Pods each use a small fraction of an NVIDIA L4 GPU, but each currently gets a whole GPU on GKE, and the GPUs sit mostly idle. The workloads tolerate sharing compute time. What should you configure?

options.A: A node pool with more GPUs per node.
options.B: Resource limits of nvidia.com/gpu: 0.25 on each Pod.
options.C: A GPU node pool with time-sharing enabled, for example gpu-sharing-strategy=time-sharing and max-shared-clients-per-gpu=4.
options.D: Spot VMs for the GPU node pool.

explanation.summary: Time-sharing presents one physical GPU as several schedulable units, so several Pods run on it in turn.

option_breakdown.A: More GPUs per node increases idle capacity.
option_breakdown.B: Kubernetes does not accept fractional GPU requests.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Time-sharing presents one physical GPU as several schedulable units, so several Pods run on it in turn.
option_breakdown.D: Spot lowers price per GPU but still gives each Pod a whole GPU.

questions.title: Hard isolation between workloads on one A100
questions.summary: Multi-instance GPUs partition an A100/H100 into isolated instances with their own memory and compute.
questions.question: Several teams share A100 GPU nodes for small inference models. Each workload must get a guaranteed slice of GPU memory and compute, isolated from the others' faults and memory use. What should you use?

options.A: GPU time-sharing.
options.B: Multi-instance GPUs, partitioning each A100 with a partition size such as 1g.5gb.
options.C: Separate namespaces with ResourceQuotas for nvidia.com/gpu.
options.D: One GPU node pool per team with the same A100 node size.

explanation.summary: Multi-instance GPU splits a supported GPU into hardware-isolated instances, each with dedicated memory and compute, which time-sharing does not provide.

option_breakdown.A: Time-sharing shares one GPU in turn with no memory or fault isolation.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Multi-instance GPU splits a supported GPU into hardware-isolated instances, each with dedicated memory and compute, which time-sharing does not provide.
option_breakdown.C: Quotas limit how many GPUs a namespace may use; they do not partition a GPU.
option_breakdown.D: Separate pools isolate teams but give each workload a whole GPU.

questions.title: An identity that belongs to one agent only
questions.summary: Agent Identity gives each agent deployed to Agent Runtime its own principal, tied to the agent's lifecycle.
questions.question: Five agents deployed to Agent Runtime in one project all use the same service identity, so audit logs cannot tell which agent read a dataset, and every agent can reach every other agent's data. What should you use instead?

options.A: One user-managed service account key per agent, bundled with its code.
options.B: A shared service account with IAM conditions on the agent's display name.
options.C: Agent Identity, so each deployed agent gets its own principal to which you grant only its own roles.
options.D: Separate Google groups for each agent's developers.

explanation.summary: Agent Identity creates a unique principal per agent, tied to its lifecycle, that works with IAM, principal access boundary policies and audit logs.

option_breakdown.A: Keys in code are a security risk and are unnecessary.
option_breakdown.B: IAM conditions cannot tell which agent is using a shared identity.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Agent Identity creates a unique principal per agent, tied to its lifecycle, that works with IAM, principal access boundary policies and audit logs.
option_breakdown.D: Developers' groups do not change the identity the agent runs as.

questions.title: Decommissioning an agent completely
questions.summary: Deleting an agent leaves its IAM bindings in place; remove them as part of decommissioning.
questions.question: An agent with its own Agent Identity was granted roles on three BigQuery datasets and a bucket. The agent is being retired. What must you do besides deleting the Agent Runtime instance?

options.A: Nothing; deleting the agent removes every binding that references it.
options.B: Disable the project's default compute service account.
options.C: Delete the agent's staging bucket to revoke its roles.
options.D: Remove the IAM bindings that reference the agent's principal, because deleting the agent does not remove them.

explanation.summary: Deleting an agent leaves bindings to its principal in the policies as inactive grants. Removing them keeps policies clean and auditable.

option_breakdown.A: Bindings are not cleaned up automatically.
option_breakdown.B: The default compute service account is unrelated to the agent's identity.
option_breakdown.C: The staging bucket holds deployment artefacts; deleting it revokes nothing.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Deleting an agent leaves bindings to its principal in the policies as inactive grants. Removing them keeps policies clean and auditable.

questions.title: BigQuery notebook runtimes on a private network
questions.summary: An administrator's runtime template fixes the network, subnet and public-IP setting for notebook runtimes.
questions.question: Analysts run Colab Enterprise notebooks in BigQuery Studio. Security requires every notebook runtime to run in the analytics VPC subnet with no public IP address. How should an administrator enforce this?

options.A: Create a runtime template with that network and subnet and public IP disabled, and have analysts use only that template.
options.B: Ask analysts to run !ip commands at the top of each notebook.
options.C: Create a firewall rule denying egress from BigQuery.
options.D: Move the notebooks into a Cloud Storage bucket in the VPC.

explanation.summary: Runtime templates define the machine and network configuration of notebook runtimes, so an administrator can standardise networking for everyone.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Runtime templates define the machine and network configuration of notebook runtimes, so an administrator can standardise networking for everyone.
option_breakdown.B: Commands inside a notebook cannot change the runtime's network.
option_breakdown.C: BigQuery is not a VM that firewall rules apply to.
option_breakdown.D: Where notebooks are stored does not decide where runtimes run.

questions.title: Collecting diagnostics from a misbehaving Workbench instance
questions.summary: gcloud workbench instances diagnose gathers logs and system data into a bucket for support.
questions.question: A Workbench instance's JupyterLab interface will not load, and Cloud Customer Care asks for system logs and diagnostics from the instance. What is the simplest way to collect them?

options.A: Run gcloud workbench instances diagnose, writing the output to a Cloud Storage bucket.
options.B: Delete and recreate the instance, then send its creation logs.
options.C: Take a screenshot of the browser error.
options.D: Export the project's billing data.

explanation.summary: The diagnose command collects system, network and JupyterLab logs from the instance and uploads them to a bucket you name.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The diagnose command collects system, network and JupyterLab logs from the instance and uploads them to a bucket you name.
option_breakdown.B: Recreating destroys the evidence.
option_breakdown.C: A screenshot does not contain the instance's logs.
option_breakdown.D: Billing data has nothing to do with the fault.

questions.title: Workstations reachable only from the corporate network
questions.summary: A private workstation cluster uses a private gateway reached through Private Service Connect.
questions.question: Security requires that Cloud Workstations cannot be reached from the public internet at all; developers connect only from the corporate network, which is linked to the VPC by Interconnect. How should the workstation cluster be created?

options.A: As a public cluster with an organisation policy on external IPs.
options.B: As a private cluster (private gateway), with a Private Service Connect endpoint in the VPC for clients.
options.C: As a public cluster with Cloud Armor in front of it.
options.D: As a public cluster where workstations have no external IP.

explanation.summary: A private cluster's gateway accepts connections only through Private Service Connect from networks connected to the VPC, not from the internet.

option_breakdown.A: That constraint limits VM external IPs; the public gateway is still reachable.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A private cluster's gateway accepts connections only through Private Service Connect from networks connected to the VPC, not from the internet.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Armor filters traffic but leaves the endpoint public.
option_breakdown.D: Workstations without external IPs can still be reached through the public gateway.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud workstations clusters create dev-private --region=europe-west1 --network=NET --subnetwork=SUBNET \
  --enable-private-endpoint
# then create a PSC endpoint in the VPC for the cluster's service attachment

questions.title: A GPU in a data scientist's workstation
questions.summary: The workstation configuration specifies the GPU; Cloud Workstations attaches it and installs drivers.
questions.question: Data scientists using Cloud Workstations need an NVIDIA T4 GPU for local model experiments. How should the platform team provide it?

options.A: Attach a GPU to each running workstation VM in Compute Engine.
options.B: Create a workstation configuration with an N1 machine type and one nvidia-tesla-t4 accelerator.
options.C: Create the configuration with an E2 machine type and a GPU.
options.D: Install the NVIDIA driver in the container image and nothing else.

explanation.summary: GPUs are declared on the workstation configuration. Only N1, A2 and A3 machine types support them, and Cloud Workstations attaches the GPU and installs its driver.

option_breakdown.A: Workstation VMs are managed by the service; editing them directly is not supported.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. GPUs are declared on the workstation configuration. Only N1, A2 and A3 machine types support them, and Cloud Workstations attaches the GPU and installs its driver.
option_breakdown.C: E2 machine types do not support GPUs.
option_breakdown.D: A driver without an attached GPU does nothing.

questions.title: Protecting a database from a Cloud Run scale-out
questions.summary: Set maximum instances so a traffic burst cannot open more database connections than the database allows.
questions.question: During a marketing burst, a Cloud Run service scaled to 400 instances and exhausted the connection limit of its Cloud SQL database, taking the whole site down. Each instance opens up to 5 connections, and the database allows 500. What should you set?

options.A: Minimum instances of 90.
options.B: Concurrency of 1 per instance.
options.C: Maximum instances of about 90 on the service, keeping total connections under the database limit.
options.D: CPU always allocated.

explanation.summary: Maximum instances caps scale-out; requests beyond capacity queue briefly or are rejected instead of overwhelming the database.

option_breakdown.A: Minimum instances keeps instances warm; it sets no ceiling.
option_breakdown.B: Lower concurrency makes Cloud Run create even more instances.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Maximum instances caps scale-out; requests beyond capacity queue briefly or are rejected instead of overwhelming the database.
option_breakdown.D: CPU allocation affects background work and billing, not how far the service scales.

questions.title: A node pool upgrade that can be rolled back quickly
questions.summary: Blue-green node pool upgrades keep the old nodes during a soak period so you can roll back.
questions.question: A node pool runs a sensitive workload. The team wants upgrades that create the new nodes first, move Pods over, and keep the old nodes for a soak period so it can roll back quickly if problems appear. Which upgrade strategy fits?

options.A: Surge upgrades with max-surge=1 and max-unavailable=0.
options.B: Disabling auto-upgrade and upgrading by hand once a year.
options.C: Blue-green node pool upgrades with a soak duration.
options.D: Deleting and recreating the node pool on each upgrade.

explanation.summary: Blue-green upgrades create a new set of nodes, drain the old ones into it, and keep the old nodes during the soak time so a rollback is fast.

option_breakdown.A: Surge upgrades replace nodes progressively and do not keep the old ones for rollback.
option_breakdown.B: Rare manual upgrades leave the cluster unpatched.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Blue-green upgrades create a new set of nodes, drain the old ones into it, and keep the old nodes during the soak time so a rollback is fast.
option_breakdown.D: Recreating the pool causes disruption and has no rollback path.

questions.title: A changed ConfigMap the Pods ignore
questions.summary: Environment variables from a ConfigMap are read at start; restart the Deployment to pick up changes.
questions.question: A Deployment reads its feature flags from a ConfigMap through environment variables. After you update the ConfigMap, running Pods still use the old values. What should you do?

options.A: Run kubectl rollout restart deployment/web so new Pods start with the updated values.
options.B: Delete the ConfigMap and create it again.
options.C: Scale the Deployment to zero and delete the namespace.
options.D: Nothing; the values update inside running containers within a minute.

explanation.summary: Environment variables are set when a container starts. A rolling restart replaces the Pods gradually, and the new ones read the updated ConfigMap.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Environment variables are set when a container starts. A rolling restart replaces the Pods gradually, and the new ones read the updated ConfigMap.
option_breakdown.B: Recreating the ConfigMap does not restart the Pods.
option_breakdown.C: Deleting the namespace destroys the application.
option_breakdown.D: Only ConfigMaps mounted as volumes refresh in place; environment variables never do.

explanation.gcloud_command:
kubectl rollout restart deployment/web -n shop
kubectl rollout status deployment/web -n shop

questions.title: Scaling workers on a Pub/Sub backlog
questions.summary: An HPA on an external metric such as a subscription's undelivered messages scales queue consumers.
questions.question: Worker Pods on GKE pull from a Pub/Sub subscription. CPU stays low even when the backlog grows to millions of messages, so a CPU-based HPA never scales. What should the HPA use instead?

options.A: Memory utilisation.
options.B: A higher maximum replica count on the CPU-based HPA.
options.C: The node pool's cluster autoscaler.
options.D: An external metric for the subscription's number of undelivered messages, with a target per replica.

explanation.summary: Queue depth measures the work waiting. An HPA on that external metric adds workers as the backlog grows and removes them as it drains.

option_breakdown.A: Memory, like CPU, does not reflect the backlog.
option_breakdown.B: The maximum does not matter if the metric never triggers scaling.
option_breakdown.C: The cluster autoscaler adds nodes for pending Pods; it does not add Pods.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Queue depth measures the work waiting. An HPA on that external metric adds workers as the backlog grows and removes them as it drains.

explanation.gcloud_command:
metrics:
- type: External
  external:
    metric:
      name: pubsub.googleapis.com|subscription|num_undelivered_messages
      selector: { matchLabels: { resource.labels.subscription_id: orders-sub } }
    target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "100" }

questions.title: Docker Hub rate limits breaking deployments
questions.summary: An Artifact Registry remote repository caches Docker Hub images inside Google Cloud.
questions.question: GKE deployments that pull public base images from Docker Hub fail during busy periods because of Docker Hub pull rate limits. What should the platform team set up?

options.A: A Cloud NAT gateway with more IP addresses.
options.B: A standard Artifact Registry repository with cleanup policies.
options.C: imagePullPolicy: Always on every Deployment.
options.D: An Artifact Registry remote repository for Docker Hub, and point image references at it.

explanation.summary: A remote repository proxies and caches the upstream registry, so repeated pulls come from Artifact Registry instead of Docker Hub.

option_breakdown.A: More egress IPs only spread the problem around.
option_breakdown.B: A standard repository holds images you push yourself; it does not proxy Docker Hub.
option_breakdown.C: Always pulling increases the number of Docker Hub requests.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A remote repository proxies and caches the upstream registry, so repeated pulls come from Artifact Registry instead of Docker Hub.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud artifacts repositories create dockerhub --location=us-central1 --repository-format=docker \
  --mode=remote-repository --remote-docker-repo=DOCKER-HUB
# image: us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/P/dockerhub/library/nginx:1.27

questions.title: Snapshots that must stay in Germany
questions.summary: Choose the snapshot storage location (region or multi-region) explicitly to meet residency rules.
questions.question: Disks in europe-west3 (Frankfurt) are snapshotted daily. By default the snapshots went to the EU multi-region, but a regulator now requires them to stay in Germany. What should you change?

options.A: Set the snapshot storage location to europe-west3 in the snapshot schedule or on each snapshot.
options.B: Create the snapshots with a CMEK key in europe-west3.
options.C: Label the snapshots with country=de.
options.D: Take machine images instead of snapshots.

explanation.summary: Snapshots are stored in a multi-region near the disk by default, but you can choose a region as the storage location.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Snapshots are stored in a multi-region near the disk by default, but you can choose a region as the storage location.
option_breakdown.B: The key location does not decide where the snapshot data lives.
option_breakdown.C: Labels do not affect placement.
option_breakdown.D: Machine images also need an explicit location, and they are not what the schedule creates.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute resource-policies create snapshot-schedule daily-de --region=europe-west3 \
  --daily-schedule --start-time=02:00 --max-retention-days=14 --storage-location=europe-west3

questions.title: Every Pending Pod across all namespaces
questions.summary: Use kubectl get pods -A with a field selector on status.phase.
questions.question: After a node pool problem, you need a list of every Pod in the cluster that is still Pending, in any namespace. Which command gives it directly?

options.A: kubectl get nodes -o wide
options.B: kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending
options.C: kubectl describe pods --namespace=default
options.D: gcloud container clusters describe CLUSTER --location=REGION

explanation.summary: -A covers all namespaces and the field selector filters on the Pod's phase.

option_breakdown.A: That lists nodes, not Pods.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. -A covers all namespaces and the field selector filters on the Pod's phase.
option_breakdown.C: That covers only one namespace and prints long descriptions.
option_breakdown.D: Cluster configuration does not list Pods.

questions.title: Moving old objects onto the new key version
questions.summary: Rotation does not re-encrypt existing data; rewrite objects so they use the new primary version.
questions.question: A CMEK key protecting a Cloud Storage bucket was rotated after a suspected exposure of the old key version. Security wants every existing object protected by the new primary version, so that the old version can eventually be destroyed. What must happen first?

options.A: Rewrite the existing objects so they are re-encrypted with the key's new primary version.
options.B: Nothing; rotation already re-encrypted every object with the new version.
options.C: Rotate the key a second time.
options.D: Change the bucket's default key to the same key name.

explanation.summary: Rotation creates a new primary version for new encryption only. Objects written earlier stay encrypted with the older version until they are rewritten.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Rotation creates a new primary version for new encryption only. Objects written earlier stay encrypted with the older version until they are rewritten.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud KMS rotation does not re-encrypt existing data.
option_breakdown.C: Another rotation adds another version and still leaves old objects on the old one.
option_breakdown.D: The default key applies to new writes; it does not touch existing objects.

questions.title: Undoing a key destruction request
questions.summary: Destroyed key versions stay in 'scheduled for destruction' (30 days by default) and can be restored meanwhile.
questions.question: An administrator scheduled the only key version protecting a production database's CMEK key for destruction yesterday, by mistake. What should you do?

options.A: Restore the key version while it is still scheduled for destruction, then re-enable it.
options.B: Nothing can be done; destruction is immediate.
options.C: Create a new key with the same name and re-encrypt the database from it.
options.D: Ask Google Cloud support to recover the destroyed key material after the period ends.

explanation.summary: A version scheduled for destruction is kept for the destruction delay (30 days by default). During that time it can be restored; afterwards its material is gone for good.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A version scheduled for destruction is kept for the destruction delay (30 days by default). During that time it can be restored; afterwards its material is gone for good.
option_breakdown.B: Destruction is delayed precisely so mistakes can be undone.
option_breakdown.C: A new key has different material and cannot decrypt the data.
option_breakdown.D: After destruction, not even Google can recover the key material.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud kms keys versions restore 1 --key=db-key --keyring=data --location=europe-west1
gcloud kms keys versions enable 1 --key=db-key --keyring=data --location=europe-west1

questions.title: Backups that ransomware and rogue admins cannot delete
questions.summary: Backup and DR Service backup vaults enforce a minimum retention that nobody can shorten.
questions.question: After a ransomware incident at a peer company, a CISO requires VM and Cloud SQL backups that nobody, including project owners, can delete or shorten for 30 days after they are taken. What should you use?

options.A: Snapshot schedules with a 30-day retention.
options.B: Backup and DR Service with a backup vault that has a 30-day enforced minimum retention.
options.C: Cloud SQL automated backups with 30 retained backups.
options.D: An IAM condition that denies delete to everyone except owners.

explanation.summary: Backup vaults store backups immutably and indelibly for the enforced retention period, whatever roles the caller holds.

option_breakdown.A: Snapshots can be deleted by anyone with permission.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Backup vaults store backups immutably and indelibly for the enforced retention period, whatever roles the caller holds.
option_breakdown.C: Automated backups disappear if the instance is deleted and can be reconfigured.
option_breakdown.D: Owners could still delete, which is the risk being addressed.

questions.title: Reading Spanner data as it was an hour ago
questions.summary: Spanner point-in-time recovery uses version_retention_period (up to 7 days) for stale reads and restores.
questions.question: A bad batch job overwrote rows in a Spanner database 40 minutes ago. The team wants to read the rows as they were before the job and write them back. The database has version_retention_period set to 1d. What should it do?

options.A: Restore last night's backup over the database.
options.B: Increase version_retention_period now, then read the old values.
options.C: Open a support case to roll back the database.
options.D: Read the rows with a timestamp bound (stale read) at a time before the job, and write them back.

explanation.summary: With a one-day retention, Spanner keeps earlier versions of the data. A read at a past timestamp returns the rows as they were, which can then be written back.

option_breakdown.A: A night-old backup loses everything written since, not just the bad job's changes.
option_breakdown.B: Raising retention now does not bring back versions already expired, and 40 minutes is within the current window anyway.
option_breakdown.C: Recovery is self-service.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. With a one-day retention, Spanner keeps earlier versions of the data. A read at a past timestamp returns the rows as they were, which can then be written back.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud spanner databases execute-sql orders --instance=prod \
  --read-timestamp=2026-09-30T09:00:00Z --sql="SELECT * FROM Accounts WHERE Region='EU'"

questions.title: Joining Cloud SQL rows with BigQuery tables in one query
questions.summary: BigQuery federated queries use EXTERNAL_QUERY through a Cloud SQL connection.
questions.question: An analyst needs today's orders from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database joined with customer segments in BigQuery, without building a pipeline that copies the orders. What should they use?

options.A: A BigQuery external table over the Cloud SQL data directory.
options.B: Query Insights on the Cloud SQL instance.
options.C: A BigQuery connection to the Cloud SQL instance and EXTERNAL_QUERY inside the BigQuery SQL.
options.D: Datastream, then wait for the next daily load.

explanation.summary: Federated queries send a query to Cloud SQL and use its results in BigQuery SQL, so live rows can be joined with warehouse tables.

option_breakdown.A: External tables read files in Cloud Storage, not a database's storage.
option_breakdown.B: Query Insights diagnoses query performance; it does not join data.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Federated queries send a query to Cloud SQL and use its results in BigQuery SQL, so live rows can be joined with warehouse tables.
option_breakdown.D: Replication pipelines are the copying the analyst wants to avoid.

questions.title: Paying for compressed bytes in BigQuery storage
questions.summary: Switching a dataset to the physical storage billing model bills compressed bytes, often far cheaper.
questions.question: A BigQuery dataset holds 400 TB of logical data that compresses about 8:1, and it is rarely updated. Storage is the largest line on the bill. What change is most likely to cut storage cost?

options.A: Move the dataset to a multi-region location.
options.B: Switch the dataset's storage billing model to physical (compressed) bytes.
options.C: Turn on table snapshots.
options.D: Set a custom daily query quota.

explanation.summary: Under the physical billing model you pay for compressed bytes (at a higher unit price), which is usually much cheaper for data that compresses well.

option_breakdown.A: Location does not reduce the bytes billed.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Under the physical billing model you pay for compressed bytes (at a higher unit price), which is usually much cheaper for data that compresses well.
option_breakdown.C: Snapshots add storage.
option_breakdown.D: Query quotas limit query spend, not storage.

questions.title: Getting back an object deleted three days ago
questions.summary: Soft delete keeps deleted objects for a retention window (7 days by default), even without versioning.
questions.question: A bucket without Object Versioning has the default soft delete policy. An important object was deleted three days ago. Can it be recovered, and how?

options.A: No: without Object Versioning, a deleted object is gone immediately.
options.B: Yes: list soft-deleted objects and restore it, because the default soft delete retention is 7 days.
options.C: Yes, but only from a machine image of the VM that uploaded it.
options.D: Yes, by asking support to recover it from Google's internal backups.

explanation.summary: Soft delete keeps deleted and overwritten objects for the bucket's retention window, whether or not versioning is enabled, so the object can be restored.

option_breakdown.A: Soft delete works independently of Object Versioning.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Soft delete keeps deleted and overwritten objects for the bucket's retention window, whether or not versioning is enabled, so the object can be restored.
option_breakdown.C: Machine images contain disks, not Cloud Storage objects.
option_breakdown.D: Recovery is self-service within the soft delete window.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud storage ls --soft-deleted gs://reports/q3.pdf
gcloud storage restore gs://reports/q3.pdf#GENERATION

questions.title: Self-managed databases in the fleet view
questions.summary: Database Center also covers databases on Compute Engine VMs, alongside managed services.
questions.question: Besides Cloud SQL and AlloyDB, a company still runs self-managed MySQL on Compute Engine VMs. The DBA lead wants those in the same fleet health view. What is true?

options.A: Only managed database services can appear in Database Center.
options.B: They must first be migrated to Cloud SQL with Database Migration Service.
options.C: Database Center can include databases running on Compute Engine VMs in its fleet view.
options.D: They appear only if the VMs are in the same project as the Cloud SQL instances.

explanation.summary: Database Center covers databases on Compute Engine VMs (MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server) in addition to the managed products, across projects.

option_breakdown.A: Its coverage is not limited to managed services.
option_breakdown.B: Migration is not a prerequisite for visibility.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Database Center covers databases on Compute Engine VMs (MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server) in addition to the managed products, across projects.
option_breakdown.D: Database Center works across projects.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Database Center > filter Product: Databases on Compute Engine

questions.title: Sending only one subnet's traffic through an inspection appliance
questions.summary: A policy-based route matches source/destination/protocol and sends matching traffic to an internal LB.
questions.question: Traffic from the subnet 10.20.0.0/24 to the internet must pass through a firewall appliance cluster behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer. Traffic from all other subnets must keep its normal path. What should you create?

options.A: A static route 0.0.0.0/0 with the appliance as next hop and a higher priority.
options.B: A Cloud NAT gateway for 10.20.0.0/24.
options.C: A firewall rule that denies egress from 10.20.0.0/24.
options.D: A policy-based route matching source 10.20.0.0/24 with the internal load balancer as next hop.

explanation.summary: Policy-based routes can match on the source range, which destination-based static routes cannot, and forward matching traffic to an internal passthrough load balancer.

option_breakdown.A: A default route applies to every subnet (or tagged VMs), not by source subnet.
option_breakdown.B: NAT translates addresses; it does not insert an appliance.
option_breakdown.C: Denying traffic is not routing it through inspection.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Policy-based routes can match on the source range, which destination-based static routes cannot, and forward matching traffic to an internal passthrough load balancer.

questions.title: A highly available next hop for a static route
questions.summary: Use an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer as next hop to spread across healthy appliances.
questions.question: A custom static route sends traffic for 172.16.0.0/12 to a single appliance VM. When that VM fails, traffic is dropped. You now run two appliance VMs. How should the route change?

options.A: Create two routes with the same priority, one per appliance VM.
options.B: Put the appliances behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer and use its forwarding rule as the route's next hop.
options.C: Use --next-hop-gateway=default-internet-gateway.
options.D: Add a second network interface to the failed VM.

explanation.summary: With an internal passthrough load balancer as the next hop, traffic goes only to backends that pass health checks, so a failed appliance is taken out automatically.

option_breakdown.A: Equal-priority routes to instances spread traffic but keep sending to a failed VM while it still exists.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. With an internal passthrough load balancer as the next hop, traffic goes only to backends that pass health checks, so a failed appliance is taken out automatically.
option_breakdown.C: The internet gateway bypasses the appliances.
option_breakdown.D: Extra interfaces do not make a failed VM healthy.

questions.title: A peered VPC that cannot see the VPN routes
questions.summary: Export custom routes on one side and import them on the other for peered VPCs to use them.
questions.question: VPC hub has an HA VPN to on-premises with dynamic routes. VPC app is peered with hub, but VMs in app cannot reach on-premises. Subnet routes work fine across the peering. What should you configure?

options.A: Create a second HA VPN from app to on-premises.
options.B: Add a static route in app pointing at the VPN tunnel in hub.
options.C: Enable Private Google Access on app's subnets.
options.D: Enable export of custom routes on hub's peering and import of custom routes on app's peering.

explanation.summary: Peering exchanges subnet routes by default. Custom routes, including dynamic routes learned over VPN, are shared only when exported by one side and imported by the other. On-premises must also learn app's ranges.

option_breakdown.A: A second VPN works but is unnecessary duplication.
option_breakdown.B: A route cannot point at a tunnel in another VPC.
option_breakdown.C: Private Google Access is for reaching Google APIs.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Peering exchanges subnet routes by default. Custom routes, including dynamic routes learned over VPN, are shared only when exported by one side and imported by the other. On-premises must also learn app's ranges.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks peerings update hub-to-app --network=hub --export-custom-routes
gcloud compute networks peerings update app-to-hub --network=app --import-custom-routes

questions.title: A GKE cluster that has run out of Pod addresses
questions.summary: Add an additional (discontiguous) Pod IPv4 range and use it for new node pools.
questions.question: A VPC-native GKE cluster cannot add nodes because its Pod secondary range is exhausted, and the range cannot be expanded because neighbouring ranges are in use. What should you do?

options.A: Recreate the cluster with a larger Pod range.
options.B: Switch the cluster to routes-based networking.
options.C: Lower the maximum Pods per node on the existing node pool in place.
options.D: Add another secondary range to the subnet and create new node pools that use it as their Pod range.

explanation.summary: GKE supports additional, discontiguous Pod ranges. New node pools can take their Pod IPs from a new secondary range, so the cluster keeps growing without being recreated.

option_breakdown.A: Recreating the cluster is disruptive and unnecessary.
option_breakdown.B: A cluster cannot be converted from VPC-native to routes-based.
option_breakdown.C: Max Pods per node cannot be changed on an existing node pool.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. GKE supports additional, discontiguous Pod ranges. New node pools can take their Pod IPs from a new secondary range, so the cluster keeps growing without being recreated.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks subnets update gke-subnet --region=us-central1 \
  --add-secondary-ranges=pods-2=10.64.0.0/14
gcloud container node-pools create pool-2 --cluster=prod --location=us-central1 --pod-ipv4-range=pods-2

questions.title: One address for a global load balancer that must never change
questions.summary: Reserve a global static external IP address and use it in the global forwarding rule.
questions.question: Customers allow-list the IP address of your global external Application Load Balancer, which you will rebuild next month. The address must stay the same. What should you do?

options.A: Reserve a regional static external IP address in us-central1.
options.B: Keep the ephemeral address by never deleting the forwarding rule.
options.C: Reserve a global static external IP address and use it in the new forwarding rule.
options.D: Use the load balancer's DNS name instead of an IP.

explanation.summary: Global load balancers need global addresses. A reserved static address stays in the project and can be attached to a new forwarding rule.

option_breakdown.A: A regional address cannot be used by a global forwarding rule.
option_breakdown.B: The rebuild will delete the forwarding rule, releasing an ephemeral address.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Global load balancers need global addresses. A reserved static address stays in the project and can be attached to a new forwarding rule.
option_breakdown.D: The customers allow-list an IP address, not a DNS name.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute addresses create shop-ip --global --ip-version=IPV4
gcloud compute forwarding-rules create shop-fr --global --address=shop-ip --target-https-proxy=shop-proxy --ports=443

questions.title: Every firewall rule that actually applies to one VM
questions.summary: get-effective-firewalls shows hierarchical, network-policy and VPC rules applying to an interface.
questions.question: A VM is subject to organisation and folder firewall policies, a global network firewall policy and VPC firewall rules. You need the combined list of rules that apply to its network interface. What should you run?

options.A: gcloud compute instances network-interfaces get-effective-firewalls VM --zone=ZONE
options.B: gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter=network=prod
options.C: gcloud compute firewall-policies list --organization=ORG_ID
options.D: gcloud compute instances describe VM --zone=ZONE

explanation.summary: The effective firewalls view combines every policy and rule that applies to the interface, from the organisation down.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The effective firewalls view combines every policy and rule that applies to the interface, from the organisation down.
option_breakdown.B: That lists VPC firewall rules only, not policies.
option_breakdown.C: That lists hierarchical policies, not what applies to the VM.
option_breakdown.D: Instance details do not include firewall rules.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute instances network-interfaces get-effective-firewalls app-1 --zone=us-central1-a

questions.title: NAT port exhaustion on a few busy VMs
questions.summary: Dynamic port allocation lets busy VMs get more NAT ports while quiet VMs keep few.
questions.question: A handful of VMs behind Cloud NAT open thousands of connections to the same API and see dropped connections, and NAT logs show OUT_OF_RESOURCES. Most other VMs use few connections. What is the best change?

options.A: Raise the static minimum ports per VM for every VM.
options.B: Remove Cloud NAT and give the busy VMs external IPs.
options.C: Enable dynamic port allocation on the NAT gateway, with a suitable maximum ports per VM.
options.D: Enable Private Google Access.

explanation.summary: Dynamic port allocation starts each VM with a minimum and grows its allocation on demand up to a maximum, so busy VMs get more ports without reserving them for everyone.

option_breakdown.A: A higher static minimum wastes NAT addresses on idle VMs.
option_breakdown.B: External IPs remove the egress controls NAT provides.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Dynamic port allocation starts each VM with a minimum and grows its allocation on demand up to a maximum, so busy VMs get more ports without reserving them for everyone.
option_breakdown.D: Private Google Access is only for Google APIs.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute routers nats update prod-nat --router=prod-router --region=us-central1 \
  --enable-dynamic-port-allocation --min-ports-per-vm=64 --max-ports-per-vm=8192

questions.title: A cryptic log entry during an incident
questions.summary: Logs Explorer can ask Gemini Cloud Assist to explain a log entry in plain language.
questions.question: During an incident, an on-call engineer finds an unfamiliar error entry from a GKE system component in Logs Explorer and does not know what it means. With Gemini Cloud Assist set up, what is the quickest help?

options.A: Create a log-based metric for the entry.
options.B: Use Explain this log entry on the entry in Logs Explorer.
options.C: Route the entry to BigQuery and query it.
options.D: Increase the log bucket's retention.

explanation.summary: Gemini Cloud Assist can summarise what a log entry means and suggest next steps, right from Logs Explorer.

option_breakdown.A: A metric counts entries; it does not explain them.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Gemini Cloud Assist can summarise what a log entry means and suggest next steps, right from Logs Explorer.
option_breakdown.C: Querying in BigQuery does not explain the message.
option_breakdown.D: Retention has nothing to do with understanding the entry.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Logs Explorer > expand the entry > Explain this log entry

questions.summary: Cloud Hub's deployments view shows recent GKE and Cloud Run deployments, including failed App Hub ones.
questions.question: Your applications are defined in App Hub. A manager asks each morning which applications had failed deployments overnight on GKE or Cloud Run. Where can you see this in one place?

options.A: Personalized Service Health.
options.B: Active Assist recommendations.
options.C: Cloud Asset Inventory history.
options.D: The Deployments page of Cloud Hub.

explanation.summary: Cloud Hub's deployments view lists recent application deployments to GKE and Cloud Run and highlights failed App Hub application deployments.

option_breakdown.A: Service Health covers Google-side incidents, not your deployments.
option_breakdown.B: Recommendations are about optimisation.
option_breakdown.C: Asset history shows configuration changes, not deployment outcomes per application.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Cloud Hub's deployments view lists recent application deployments to GKE and Cloud Run and highlights failed App Hub application deployments.

questions.summary: Cloud Hub's Optimization page shows cost and utilisation per project or App Hub application.
questions.question: The checkout application, defined in App Hub, uses resources in three projects. A product owner wants its total cost trend and its most expensive workloads without writing billing queries. Where should they look?

options.D: The Personalized Service Health dashboard.

option_breakdown.B: Correct. Cloud Hub summarises cost and utilisation for a project or an App Hub application, including its trend and its top workloads by cost.
option_breakdown.C: Database Center covers databases only.
option_breakdown.D: Service Health shows Google incidents.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Cloud Hub > Optimization > Application: checkout

questions.title: Paging on how fast the error budget is burning
questions.summary: An SLO burn-rate alert pages when the error budget is being consumed too quickly.
questions.question: A service has a 99.9% availability SLO over 28 days in Cloud Monitoring. The team wants to be paged when errors are consuming the error budget fast enough to exhaust it long before the period ends, not on every small blip. What alert should it create?

options.A: A burn-rate alerting policy on the SLO.
options.B: A threshold alert on any HTTP 5xx.
options.C: An uptime check from three regions.
options.D: A log-based alert on every error entry.

explanation.summary: Burn-rate alerts compare the current rate of budget consumption with the rate that would exactly use it up, which ignores small blips but catches serious trends.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Burn-rate alerts compare the current rate of budget consumption with the rate that would exactly use it up, which ignores small blips but catches serious trends.
option_breakdown.B: Any 5xx pages on blips, the noise to avoid.
option_breakdown.C: Uptime checks test reachability, not budget consumption.
option_breakdown.D: Per-error alerts are even noisier.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Monitoring > Services > checkout > SLO > Create SLO alert: burn rate 10 over a 1-hour lookback

questions.title: Testing a multi-step checkout journey every five minutes
questions.summary: Synthetic monitors run scripted tests (such as browser flows) on a schedule and alert on failure.
questions.question: An uptime check confirms the shop's home page returns 200, but last week the checkout flow broke while the home page stayed up. The team wants a scripted test that logs in, adds an item and checks out every five minutes. What should it use?

options.A: A synthetic monitor in Cloud Monitoring running a scripted browser test.
options.B: An uptime check on the checkout URL.
options.C: A log-based metric on checkout errors.
options.D: Cloud Trace sampling at 100%.

explanation.summary: Synthetic monitors run your test code on a schedule, including multi-step browser flows, and report results and failures to Cloud Monitoring for alerting.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Synthetic monitors run your test code on a schedule, including multi-step browser flows, and report results and failures to Cloud Monitoring for alerting.
option_breakdown.B: An uptime check requests one URL; it cannot log in and complete a flow.
option_breakdown.C: A log metric depends on real users hitting the failure first.
option_breakdown.D: Tracing shows latency of real requests; it does not test flows.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Monitoring > Synthetic monitoring > Create synthetic monitor > Mocha/Puppeteer template, every 5 min

questions.title: An uptime check for a service with no public address
questions.summary: Private uptime checks reach internal endpoints through Service Directory.
questions.question: An internal HR API runs behind an internal load balancer with no external IP. The team wants an uptime check and alert on it like its public services. What should it configure?

options.A: A public uptime check against the internal IP address.
options.B: A private uptime check targeting the API through a Service Directory endpoint.
options.C: An external IP on the load balancer for the uptime checkers only.
options.D: A VM running curl in a cron job.

explanation.summary: Private uptime checks reach internal resources through Service Directory, with firewall rules for the checkers' ranges, so the API stays internal.

option_breakdown.A: Public checkers cannot reach private IP addresses.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Private uptime checks reach internal resources through Service Directory, with firewall rules for the checkers' ranges, so the API stays internal.
option_breakdown.C: Exposing the API defeats its internal design.
option_breakdown.D: A self-built checker is extra infrastructure without uptime-check reporting.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud service-directory services create hr-api --namespace=internal --location=us-central1
# Monitoring > Uptime checks > Create > Internal IP (Service Directory service hr-api)

questions.title: Existing Grafana dashboards on Managed Service for Prometheus
questions.summary: Grafana queries Managed Service for Prometheus with PromQL through a Cloud Monitoring data source.
questions.question: A team moved from self-managed Prometheus to Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus but wants to keep its Grafana dashboards, which use PromQL. What should it do?

options.A: Rewrite every dashboard in MQL.
options.B: Keep running the old Prometheus servers only for Grafana.
options.C: Export metrics to BigQuery and query them from Grafana with SQL.
options.D: Point Grafana at Managed Service for Prometheus through its Prometheus-compatible query API, keeping the PromQL queries.

explanation.summary: Managed Service for Prometheus supports PromQL through a Prometheus-compatible API, so Grafana dashboards keep working with a data source change.

option_breakdown.A: No rewrite is needed; PromQL is supported.
option_breakdown.B: Running old servers defeats the move.
option_breakdown.C: SQL rewrites are unnecessary.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Managed Service for Prometheus supports PromQL through a Prometheus-compatible API, so Grafana dashboards keep working with a data source change.

explanation.gcloud_command:
# Deploy the data source syncer so Grafana's Prometheus data source authenticates to
# https://monitoring.googleapis.com/v1/projects/P/location/global/prometheus

questions.title: OpenTelemetry-instrumented services on Google Cloud
questions.summary: Send OpenTelemetry metrics and traces to Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace through an OpenTelemetry Collector.
questions.question: A team instruments its services with OpenTelemetry SDKs so it is not tied to one vendor. It wants the metrics in Cloud Monitoring and the traces in Cloud Trace, without changing the instrumentation. What should it deploy?

options.A: The Ops Agent's legacy Monitoring agent configuration only.
options.B: Rewrite the instrumentation with the Cloud Monitoring client library.
options.C: An OpenTelemetry Collector (for example the Google-built collector) that exports to Google Cloud.
options.D: Log-based metrics on the application's stdout.

explanation.summary: An OpenTelemetry Collector receives OTLP from the SDKs and exports metrics and traces to Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace, so the code stays vendor-neutral.

option_breakdown.A: That collects VM system metrics, not the application's OTLP telemetry.
option_breakdown.B: Rewriting ties the code to one vendor, which the team wants to avoid.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. An OpenTelemetry Collector receives OTLP from the SDKs and exports metrics and traces to Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace, so the code stays vendor-neutral.
option_breakdown.D: Log parsing loses the structured metrics and traces.

explanation.gcloud_command: # collector config: receivers: otlp; exporters: googlecloud (traces), googlemanagedprometheus (metrics)

questions.title: VPC Flow Logs costing more than they are worth
questions.summary: Lower the sampling rate and lengthen the aggregation interval to reduce flow log volume.
questions.question: VPC Flow Logs on a busy subnet are used for weekly traffic analysis, but their volume has become a large part of the logging bill. Exact per-connection records are not needed. What should you change?

options.A: Lower the subnet's flow log sampling rate and increase its aggregation interval.
options.B: Disable flow logs and rely on firewall rules logging.
options.C: Route flow logs to a bucket with 1-day retention.
options.D: Enable Data Access audit logs instead.

explanation.summary: Sampling and aggregation settings control how many flow records are generated, which cuts volume and cost while keeping the traffic picture.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Sampling and aggregation settings control how many flow records are generated, which cuts volume and cost while keeping the traffic picture.
option_breakdown.B: Firewall logs cover only traffic matched by logged rules.
option_breakdown.C: Shorter retention still pays to ingest every record.
option_breakdown.D: Audit logs record API calls, not network flows.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks subnets update web --region=us-central1 \
  --logging-flow-sampling=0.1 --logging-aggregation-interval=interval-5-min

questions.title: What TERMINATED means in the instance list
questions.summary: TERMINATED means stopped, not deleted: the VM still exists and its disks and reserved addresses still cost money.
questions.question: While checking what is running in a project, you see a VM reported with the status TERMINATED in the output of gcloud compute instances list. A teammate assumes the VM has been deleted and that nothing about it is still billed. What is actually true?

options.A: The VM was deleted, and it stays in the list for 30 days before it disappears.
options.B: The VM is stopped. It can be started again, and its persistent disks are still billed.
options.C: The VM crashed and Compute Engine will restart it automatically within the hour.
options.D: The VM is suspended, and its memory contents are preserved and billed until it resumes.

explanation.summary: In Compute Engine, TERMINATED is the state of a stopped VM. A deleted VM is not listed at all. You stop paying for vCPUs and memory, but attached disks and static IP addresses continue to be charged.

option_breakdown.A: A deleted instance no longer appears in the list; there is no 30-day listing period.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. TERMINATED is the stopped state: the instance resource remains, it can be started, and its disks keep costing money.
option_breakdown.C: Stopping does not schedule a restart, and TERMINATED does not by itself mean a crash. Automatic restart applies when a VM configured for it crashes or Compute Engine stops it for a programmed stop, such as a maintenance event.
option_breakdown.D: A suspended VM is reported as SUSPENDED, a different state from TERMINATED.

questions.title: Every VM in the organization, not one project
questions.summary: gcloud compute instances list is scoped to one project; Cloud Asset Inventory searches across an organization.
questions.question: A security review needs a single list of every Compute Engine instance across all of the several hundred projects in your organization. You want to avoid writing a script that loops over projects. What should you use?

options.A: gcloud compute instances list --all-projects
options.B: The VM instances page of the Google Cloud console, with a filter on the organization name
options.C: gcloud asset search-all-resources with the organization as the scope and the Compute Engine instance asset type
options.D: A Cloud Billing export to BigQuery, querying the Compute Engine rows by project

explanation.summary: Cloud Asset Inventory searches resources across a project, folder or organization scope, so with the search permission granted on the organization, one command covers every project under it.

option_breakdown.A: gcloud compute instances list has no flag that spans all projects; it works on one project at a time.
option_breakdown.B: The VM instances page shows the instances of the selected project.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. search-all-resources accepts an organization scope and can be limited to compute.googleapis.com/Instance.
option_breakdown.D: Billing data records charges and SKUs, not an inventory of the instances that currently exist.

questions.title: Applying a lifecycle configuration from a file
questions.summary: A lifecycle configuration is a bucket-level JSON document, applied with gcloud storage buckets update --lifecycle-file.
questions.question: You wrote a JSON file containing the lifecycle rules for an existing bucket that stores build artifacts. You want the rules to take effect on the bucket from now on. Which command applies them?

options.A: gcloud storage objects update gs://build-artifacts/** --lifecycle-file=rules.json
options.B: gcloud storage buckets update gs://build-artifacts --lifecycle-file=rules.json
options.C: gcloud storage cp rules.json gs://build-artifacts/.lifecycle
options.D: gcloud storage buckets create gs://build-artifacts --lifecycle=rules.json

explanation.summary: Lifecycle configuration belongs to the bucket, not to individual objects, so it is set by updating the bucket with the JSON file.

option_breakdown.A: Lifecycle rules are not an object property, so an object-level update cannot set them.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. buckets update with --lifecycle-file sets the bucket's lifecycle configuration from the file's contents.
option_breakdown.C: Copying a file into a bucket only stores it as an object; no special file name configures the bucket.
option_breakdown.D: The bucket already exists, and create would fail rather than change its configuration.

questions.title: A live-only age rule that never frees versioned storage
questions.summary: With Object Versioning on, a Delete rule limited to isLive true only makes live objects noncurrent; removing those versions needs a rule that can match them.
questions.question: A bucket has Object Versioning enabled and one lifecycle rule: Delete when age is 365 days and isLive is true. A year later the rule is clearly firing, because old objects no longer show in a normal listing, yet the bucket's stored bytes keep growing. What should you change?

options.A: Move the bucket to the Archive class, because lifecycle deletions do not apply to Standard objects.
options.B: Disable Object Versioning, which permanently removes all existing noncurrent versions.
options.C: Replace the lifecycle rule with a nightly script that deletes the old objects by name.
options.D: Add a rule that deletes noncurrent versions, for example with a daysSinceNoncurrentTime condition.

explanation.summary: On a versioned bucket, a Delete action applied to a live object turns it into a noncurrent version, which keeps being stored and billed. This rule requires isLive to be true, so it never matches those versions. Without that condition, an age rule would also delete noncurrent versions past that age on a later run.

option_breakdown.A: Lifecycle actions apply in every storage class, and Archive would add retrieval costs without removing anything.
option_breakdown.B: Disabling versioning stops new versions being kept but leaves existing noncurrent versions in place.
option_breakdown.C: A script deleting live objects has the same effect as the rule and leaves the same noncurrent versions behind.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. daysSinceNoncurrentTime is satisfied once a version has been noncurrent for the set number of days, so the rule removes the versions consuming the storage. numNewerVersions alone would not clear them all, because the newest noncurrent version of an object with no live version has no newer versions.

questions.title: Deleting Coldline objects after a month
questions.summary: Each colder class has a minimum storage duration; deleting early is charged as if the object stayed the full minimum.
questions.question: To lower storage cost, a team stores temporary exports in Coldline Storage and deletes each export 30 days after writing it. The exports are almost never read. When you review the estimate, what should you point out?

options.A: Coldline bills only for the 30 days stored, so the estimate only needs to compare the per-GB rates.
options.B: Objects deleted before the Coldline minimum are rejected, so the 30-day deletion will fail.
options.C: Each export is charged as if it were stored for Coldline's 90-day minimum, so a warmer class may be cheaper.
options.D: Coldline has no minimum duration, but each deletion costs the same as retrieving the whole object.

explanation.summary: Nearline, Coldline and Archive have minimum storage durations of 30, 90 and 365 days. Early deletion is allowed, and it is charged as though the object had been stored for the full minimum.

option_breakdown.A: This ignores the minimum duration, which is what makes short-lived data expensive in a cold class.
option_breakdown.B: Early deletion succeeds; the consequence is a charge, not an error.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Thirty days in Coldline is billed as 90, so a warmer class such as Nearline, whose minimum is only 30 days, can cost less for this pattern. Compare the rates for your location.
option_breakdown.D: Coldline does have a minimum duration, and the charge is for the remaining storage time rather than a retrieval.
